utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We continue this morning to hear the closing arguments for Mr. Ojdanic presented by Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, yesterday we were talking about General Ojdanic's advocacy of the limited use of the army, his belief that the MUP should be used to protect the population, and his belief, similar or if not more restrained, than that of General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic concerning the constrained use of the army, lest [Realtime transcript read in error "less"] that lead to war, and in his military expert report, General Radinovic concluded from the collegium of 10 July 1998 that, "General Ojdanic opposes this direct use of the VJ for the defence of the civilian population in settlements, for that would surely lead to a general war in Kosovo and Metohija." By the same token in a collegium of 19 June 1998, General Ojdanic stated that with respect to the establishment of a reserve army unit in Serbia proper to possibly assist in operations in Kosovo, he said, "I don't think that we could take a unit from Serbia and send it down there without a decision by responsible organs." That's P921 at page 15. In the collegium of 24 August 1998, 3D513, General Dimitrijevic stated that the VJ was then "being engaged quite extensively" with the MUP and anti-terrorist operations. General Dimitrijevic was concerned about that because he thought it "could be quite a strong reason to decide to launch air-strikes." That's at page 11. General Ojdanic, after noting that in his opinion VJ units "are engaged too much outside the border area" at page 13 said as follows: "General Aco," meaning General Dimitrijevic, "was right to ask that question and that is about the extensive use of the VJ working with the MUP. And he goes on to say, "It turned out that throughout this territory, that is in inland areas which are practically areas of fields, it's Yugoslav army units which are in charge which in view of the remarks made here is not good." General Ojdanic then specifically agreed with General Dimitrijevic that in view of these developments air-strikes could be "nearing fast" as he put it and warned against this more extensive use of the VJ working with MUP and anti-terrorist operations. And the Trial Chamber will recall the testimony of General Dimitrijevic in an answer to a question by Judge Bonomy. General Dimitrijevic stated that before both and after becoming Chief of the General Staff General Ojdanic "insisted that the army should be in the function provided by the constitution and bylaws." So I don't think he differed on that score either, namely that the worst way of using the military was exactly the way it was being used. Judge Bonomy, not being satisfied that this answer was specific enough to his question further stated, "Was he, General Ojdanic, against, as you were, the extensive use of the military in the fight against terrorism?" General Dimitrijevic responded, "I think he was, Mr. President." That's at TR 26732. And that is indeed what the record shows. This makes even more nonsensical the OTP's baseless claim in paragraph 768 of its brief that "On 25 December 1998, Ojdanic proposed the removal of 3rd Army commander Samardzic who had been critical of the VJ's role in internal operations." The record references cited by the OTP do not support that declaration, and it's clear in any event that General Ojdanic was solidly in line with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic on the VJ's limited role in internal operations. And I think the Trial Chamber will recall that General Samardzic became the Chief Inspector of the army. He took a very active part in the collegiums after leaving as commander of the 3rd Army. That, I don't believe in any way was a demotion for him as implied by the OTP. The short of it is that the Prosecution is wrong when it asserts that General Ojdanic was someone who was willing to use the army in a less limited and restrained manner than advocated by General Perisic or for that matter General Dimitrijevic. As we have shown, the truth is to the contrary, and there is no evidence which indicates that General Ojdanic, when he became chief of staff, was any more willing to use the VJ than was absolutely necessary to repel KLA provocations and attacks and to prepare for NATO air attacks or a potential land invasion. And I won't repeat here the extensive evidence cited in our brief concerning the members of the General Staff uniformly testifying that there was no change of policy when General Ojdanic succeeded General Perisic as the army's chief of staff. Turning to another area. The OTP alleges that General Ojdanic pre-war attempt to violate international agreements is shown by the actions taken by him to deal with KLA provocations and operations during the period when he was the deputy chief of staff. Again, we suggest that the OTP has it wrong. I believe the most logical place to start this discussion is the collegium of 10 July 1998, which is 3D641. At that time, General Ojdanic stated, page 2: "As far as an anti-terrorist operation is concerned, I am not aware of such an operation, but I would like to stress that since General Dimitrijevic, and we all know that military and diplomatic representatives are now permanently stationed in the area, they will carefully record all developments in Kosovo and Metohija, including the engagement of the units of the Serbian MUP and the Yugoslav army." So as late as 10 July 1998, General Ojdanic, as he put it, "was not aware of such an anti-terrorist operation." And the reason that he was unaware of this operation was made known by the immediately following speaker at that collegium, General Dimitrijevic, who said, "As far as anti-terrorist activities are concerned, they are being carried out too, and taking all these things into consideration they have been planned so that the MUP forces never appear as initiators but always responding to attacks. I said nothing about this, yet it is already being done down there." So there it is in a nutshell, Your Honours. Dimitrijevic stating that he had said nothing about an anti-terrorist operation, thereby confirming the evidence we've heard in this trial that General Ojdanic knew little, if anything, about such an operation until the day of that collegium, 10 July 1998. The Trial Chamber will also recall the evidence concerning General Ojdanic's complaint that he was not kept advised about combat operations, and the testimony of General Radinovic, the military expert, that General Ojdanic had a rather cold relationship with General Perisic, not helped at all by General Perisic's veto of General Ojdanic's proposed Ph.D. thesis on a military subject that was, at least according to Radinovic, worthy of respect. Both in his testimony and expert report General Radinovic confirmed General Ojdanic's lack of awareness of both combat and anti-terrorism operations, that's 3D1116, pages 77, 79, as did General Obradovic, who testified that General Ojdanic did not attend any meetings or sign any documents pertaining to either the promulgation of the 28 July 1998 anti-terrorism directive of General Perisic or its execution. That's at 14942-43. I think it's fair to say that before becoming chief of staff the primary, if not the only significant reference by General Ojdanic to anti-terrorist activities came when, as the deputy chief of staff, General Ojdanic briefed the military attaches on 27 August 1998, a meeting attended by Colonel John Crosland. This is another area where both the Prosecution and Colonel Crosland got a wrong. It was the long-time position of Colonel Crosland, from the time of his first statement to the OTP in 1998 and continuing through both the Milosevic trial and this trial, that he had shown a video to General Ojdanic including joint attacks on Albanian villages by combined VJ and MUP forces. During the trial Ms. Carter for the Prosecution asked Colonel Crosland: "Q. Just to be clear on the time line, prior to your handing the video over to Ojdanic and saying 'look, this is a joint operation, what was the party line in regards to whether the MUP and the VJ were acting separately or together.' "A. "The party line on the whole was that there was -- there was no collusion between the VJ and the MUP. "Q. Okay. At the point that you then hand the video to Ojdanic and put it to his face, is that when the party line changes and there's acknowledgement on behalf of the VJ as a whole that there are joint operations? "A. I think there was. No, I don't think there was. There was a resignation that they had been given factual evidence that was correct and difficult to refute but they didn't wish to acknowledge that evidence per se." That's at 9789, 9790. We now know that Colonel Crosland finally admitted during my cross-examination that he did not show this video to General Ojdanic personally, contrary to his prior statements and testimony but, rather, he had "probably" given the video to Colonel Negovan Jovanovic, the officer in charge of liaison duties with military attaches. That's at 9891. The Trial Chamber will also recall the firm testimony of Colonel Jovanovic that no such video was shown either to him or any member of his staff. That's at 14911. And when I think of the word agony used by you, Judge Bonomy, in describing whether or not to admit the Perisic written interview, think of the agony experienced by General Ojdanic, knowing for all these years that the written statement given by Colonel Crosland and his trial testimony was either mistaken or false, however you want to characterise it. Think of how he felt, how General Ojdanic felt when Ms. Carter rather bluntly asked Colonel Crosland about "putting the video to Ojdanic's face." What makes this matter even more sobering was Crosland's finally admitting that he did not give the video to General Ojdanic. It happened purely by chance, as Judge Bonomy noted at the time. It had nothing whatever to do with the skill of my cross-examination but was just a piece of good fortune. And that again shows how easy it is to get it wrong and the fragility of our criminal justice system. You will also recall that Colonel Crosland further admitted, contrary to his earlier written statements and testimony in the Milosevic trial, that Mr. Paddy Ashdown did not show General Ojdanic photos of joint VJ/MUP operations in the fall of 1998, but Colonel Crosland did testify under oath erroneously in that respect at the Milosevic trial, and in that case there was no calling it back. Again on the subject of General Ojdanic's pre-war intent, I would like now to turn to the Prosecution's argument that General Ojdanic knew of crimes committed by FRY and Serb forces operating in Kosovo in 1998 when he was the deputy chief of staff. That's OTP paragraph 787-788. According to the Prosecution, this made General Ojdanic aware that the units allegedly committing such crimes would continue to commit them during the indictment period. The fact is, however, that the Prosecution did not prove the commission of any specific crimes by Serb forces in the year 1988 [sic], let alone that General Ojdanic knew of such alleged crimes. The only two paragraphs of the OTP brief devoted to this issue, 787, 788, do not mention the commission of crimes by Serb forces but at most the excessive use of force. In paragraph 787, the Prosecution talks not about crimes but, rather, the evidence of Colonel Crosland at the 27 August 1998 defence attache briefing that excessive force was allegedly used by combined VJ-MUP forces in the Prilep-Glodjane area which had created a humanitarian crisis to which General Ojdanic agreed. We have already discussed the alleged use by Serb forces of disproportionate force on pages 52 to 62 of our brief. In addition, General Ojdanic's comments at the Defence attache meeting in August 1998 that "force would be met with force" was made necessary by an increasing KLA threat that was commensurate with the situation. Colonel Crosland testified that from a military point of view this made sense at transcript 9803. The other paragraph in the OTP --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down a bit for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other paragraph in the OTP brief on the alleged commission of crimes in 1998 is also concerned not with crimes but with the "international community's expressed concern about the level of violence in Kosovo." That's paragraph 788 of the Prosecution's brief. The statement is made in the OTP brief that "Ojdanic was aware of these concerns via HRW reports," paragraph 788. This is another major stretch to the breaking point by the OTP. As evidence of General Ojdanic's awareness, the OTP refers to a letter of 20 July 1998 sent by Human Rights Watch to various Serbian government departments including the VJ. The Trial Chamber may recall that Mr. Fred Abrahams testified about sending this letter. The letter is P544, which is faxed to the VJ, care of the "Kosovo -- Kosovo command Information Service," and which contained general requests for information about VJ forces, some of which pertain to obviously confidential information. The letter was sent during a vacation period, and the recipient, whomever it may have been, was given ten days to reply at a time when the VJ had its hands full in combatting terrorist activities. There's absolutely nothing in this letter, as you will see when you look at it, which supports the OTP claim that General Ojdanic, then the deputy chief of staff, ever received or looked at this letter or was made aware of the letter. Rather than spend more time on this I would simply refer the Trial Chamber to my cross-examination of Mr. Abrahams at pages 892 to 899 which I believe gives you perhaps more than you would ever want to know on this subject, which is really of no substance to the case and should not have been mentioned at all by the OTP except as another illustration of the weakness of its case. Another matter that we must mention in the interests of getting it right is the OTP's misleading claim which quotes some comments of General Andjelkovic who was the General Staff's chief of sector for communications and electronic operations. General Andjelkovic states as follows at a collegium of 2 February 1999, and this is quoted by the OTP in its brief at paragraph 260. The quote says: "If it is true that the subordinates are doing what they shouldn't be doing and sending us reports saying that they did not do it and we have adequate or accurate information that they did not do it -- that they did do it and that nobody has been held responsible, I cannot possibly accept that, and I think that people are right when they raise the question of our competence." The OTP presumably implies by offering this comment of General Andjelkovic that this refers to some failure to report a crime or some other improper similar conduct. What the OTP fails to refer to is the specific explanation of this portion of the collegium given by General Andjelkovic in his trial testimony at 16400-401 where he says, this very quote that we're talking about now, he says, "This was about the too liberal use of mobile phones and hand-held radio sets. We sent out warnings. We warned subordinate units to try to stop this type of equipment from being misused. No one paid any heed, especially the MUP units. That's why I raise the issue. Were we sufficiently competent to issue an order that would put a stop to this sort of practice, that's what it was about." This testimony followed earlier testimony by General Andjelkovic that the KLA was monitoring movements by FRY forces through conversations over mobile phones and hand-held sets. That's TR 16399. So that was the purpose of General Andjelkovic's comments at the collegium. And unless it was just missed by the OTP, it's really difficult to understand why the OTP omitted this explanation from their brief, especially since the OTP gets it wrong again by mentioning the same alleged misreporting in paragraph 835, footnote 2101 of its brief. Now, I'd like to spend a bit more time on the period when General Ojdanic became Chief of the General Staff on 27 November 1998 to the beginning of the war. We know from the evidence that Serbian forces, following their summer offensive against the KLA, had succeeded in recapturing most of the territory previously occupied by the KLA. We're also aware of the considerable body of evidence starting in the fall of 1998 and continuing to the start of the war in March 1999 that terrorist attacks and provocations continued and indeed escalated in violation of the cease-fire and that the KLA occupied the territory it had previously abandoned. So these were the harsh realities facing General Ojdanic when he assumed command of the General Staff on 27 a November 1998. He had to ensure that the VJ fulfilled its responsibilities under the October agreements and at the same time respond to the continuing threat posed by the actions and provocations of the KLA and the threat of bombing and potentially a land invasion by NATO. We say he responded honourably and humanely in matters large and small. Whether it be Podujevo or Racak or his decision not to draft students of military schools and use them in VJ units, all of which and much more we have covered in our brief. Contrary to the arguments of the OTP, we submit that every action taken by General Ojdanic and the General Staff during this period was a legitimate response to KLA threats and provocations and/or the build-up of potential -- and potential threat from NATO forces. Again we've covered this in our brief but I do want to mention a few matters. In its brief, the OTP argues in paragraph 744-747, that General Ojdanic supported the policy of arming non-Albanians. Specifically paragraph 744 states that: "Ojdanic did not reverse but continued the practice of arming non-Albanian civilians despite being informed of the danger they posed." This assertion is entirely erroneous and unsupported by a citation to the evidence in this case. The fact is that there was no further arming of non-Albanian civilians after General Ojdanic took over as chief of staff. Further, the OTP twists a good faith effort of General Ojdanic to include armed Serbs in the wartime establishment. His goal was to bring them into the system so that they could be accounted for instead of operating as freelance soldiers. This issue is discussed in considerable detail in paragraphs 22 to 54 of our final brief. On Tuesday Mr. Hannis tried to link the indictment crimes to General Ojdanic by tracing events from General Ojdanic's directive of 16 January 1999, known as Grom 3. Mr. Hannis then discussed a number of Joint Command orders and areas of Kosovo where crimes are alleged to have been committed. Judge Bonomy asked whether every event Mr. Hannis described was related to -- to the Grom 3 directive. Mr. Hannis responded that this was his position. We've covered Grom 3 in detail in paragraphs 196 to 203 of our brief. Our position is simple. Grom 3 was an entirely legitimate and necessary measure aimed at the significant threats faced by the -- by the FRY. The Trial Chamber need only look at the words of the directive. It was not aimed at the expulsion of ethnic Albanian civilians or any criminal act. The Prosecution has completely failed to relate Grom 3 to the alleged JCE or anything illegal. Indeed, the parts of Grom 3 which Mr. Hannis seemed to be concerned about, the plan to destroy terrorist forces also appear in General Perisic's directive from the previous summer. In the event of an attack from NATO, the VJ had to defend the country and fight a war on two fronts. This has nothing to do with the expulsion of civilians. Similarly with regard to General Ojdanic's directive of 9 April 1999, this had nothing to do with the expulsion of Albanian civilians. Quite the opposite. At the end of our -- of his submissions, Mr. Hannis requested that the Trial Chamber look at events chronologically to understand orders by what else was happening at the time. We agree, and I refer later to the collegium of the same day when General -- where General Ojdanic emphasises that refugees should be allowed to return to their homes. I also refer later on, a bit later on, to General Ojdanic's announcement of two days beforehand on April 7, 1999, that Albanians should return to their homes and work together for peace. The Prosecution next claims an alleged bad faith VJ troop build-up in 1999. The threat to the sovereignty of the FRY by the KLA was severe and has been well documented in this case. Bislim Zyrapi, the KLA chief of staff at the relevant time, testified that in March 1999 the KLA was 17.000, 18.000 members strong and controlled a significant part of the territory of Kosovo. Leaving aside the ruthless tactics of this terrorist organisation the KLA of course represented a legitimate military target. Moreover, while the VJ complied with the October agreements, the KLA reoccupied positions previously withdrawn from as they became "more opportunistic," according to General DZ and a host of other witnesses as we've set forth in our brief. By the way, that "more opportunistic" comment of General DZ is at P2508, paragraph 189. While the threat from the KLA was extremely credible, the potential for a NATO land invasion and/or bombing campaign weighed heavily on the minds of the VJ General Staff. In the collegium at 18 February 1999, in response to the fact that NATO would be increasing troops in Macedonia to 8.000, General Ojdanic explained, "We must defend the country if we are attacked. Politics and diplomacy will do everything to resolve by peaceful means if possible." P937, page 16. The following month on 11 March General Ojdanic addressed an argument he expected to see from the West in regards to lack of compliance with the October agreements. General Ojdanic said that the OSCE knew full well, while the VJ had deployed more troops in the area. He explained that, "NATO is getting 9.500 people on board down there. We don't know whether they will use them to invade, but we can't sit here and be unprepared." P935, page 1. In addition, there was credible information that pointed to a collective effort on behalf of the KLA and NATO. This included but was not limited to the KLA being supplied with weapons by NATO, Exhibit 3D1035, paragraph 2.1, and terrorist forces being trained by NATO, Exhibit 3D584, page 2. The Trial Chamber will also recall the testimony of General Dimitrijevic in this regard. It's also noteworthy that Prosecution witness John Crosland testified that the international community had a regime change in mind for Kosovo and that the KLA was a tool to facilitate this change, as Mr. O'Sullivan reminded us yesterday, and that's at TR9865-66, Exhibit 3D510, paragraph 25. Further discussion on this alleged bad faith build-up of troops by the VJ is addressed in paragraphs 85 to 97 of our final brief. One further matter I'd like to mention during this period preceding the war is the testimony of General Dimitrijevic. This primarily concerns whether General Ojdanic was receiving accurate reports from the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps subordinates on whether provocations in violation of the cease-fire came from the KLA or whether these provocations were initiated by Serb forces. The only two specific incidents mentioned by Dimitrijevic both in the collegium and here at the trial are Podujevo and Racak. As to Podujevo, General Dimitrijevic testified that, after a general staff investigation this was indeed a legitimate training exercise, and as to Racak, General Dimitrijevic further testified that the army was not involved and that General Ojdanic insisted on knowing the truth about these events. No other specific incident was mentioned by Dimitrijevic and there is no basis in the evidence to conclude that action by Serb forces were any different than the legitimate actions revealed by both Podujevo and Racak. In any event, General Curcin answered General Dimitrijevic's question on this issue during the collegium by stating that his reports to the General Staff accurately reflected the subordinate reports. The testimony of General Obradovic of the General Staff is also pertinent here. That's at 15107. And there was a question on cross-examination by Mr. Stamp, and the question was to General Obradovic, "There again we see General Dimitrijevic suggesting that the reports coming from the Pristina Corps were not necessarily accurate about the activities of the corps. Is that a correct conclusion, that the security chief of the VJ was saying that these Pristina Corps reports are not necessarily accurate about the activities of the Pristina Corps?" And the answer was: "The thesis advocated here by General Dimitrijevic, as you can see he received this information from some sources in the West," and a brief interjection here. You'll recall the testimony of both Colonel Crosland and General Dimitrijevic that they would meet frequently. That was clearly established by the evidence. So going on with General Obradovic's answer: "He received this information from some sources in the West. So this thesis is very present in the West, that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping up operations. That's the theory. And it's a fact that the Chief of the General Staff and the collegium as a whole insisted on knowing the full truth of the situation in the units." So what General Dimitrijevic is saying is nothing new. "It's not that we didn't want or didn't know. There was no reason for us not to trust the subordinate commanders and the subordinate commands. We had no reason to doubt each and every piece of information we received. We had no reason to think it was unreliable." Moreover, as we've stated in our brief, General Ojdanic, as well as General Curcin and others took steps during the collegiums involved to heed the admonitions of General Dimitrijevic by continuing to closely monitor the accuracy of reports and issuing orders to make sure this happened. General Ojdanic further stated in the relevant collegium that he would speak to the 3rd Army commander about this issue, and as General Dimitrijevic testified, when General Ojdanic said he intended to accomplish a task, he followed through on it. Indeed the lack of any improper intent on the part of General Ojdanic was testified to by General Dimitrijevic himself, who stated that General Ojdanic was "angry" when he received inaccurate information and that he sincerely wanted to determine the truth and do the right thing. And the only person who really raised the reporting issue, General Dimitrijevic, was as categorical as the other members of the General Staff in testifying that no plan to deport Kosovar Albanians ever existed. And I'd like to use General Dimitrijevic's denial of any plan to expel Kosovar Albanians as a transition to an ultimate question in this case, which is why the refugees left Kosovo. As we explain in our brief at pages 125 to 128, and as discussed in the briefs of the other defendants, there are a number of possible explanations based on the evidence. One, the fact and the threat of NATO bombing. Two, both the fact and the prospect of combat between Serb forces and the KLA. Three, action by the KLA to move civilians to create a humanitarian crisis and to further use civilians as a shield against Serb forces. And four, individuals acting from hatred, revenge, or some other ignoble motive. There's evidence in the case as set forth in various Defence briefs to support each of these four different causes I have mentioned. Specifically as to General Ojdanic, it's clear that he believed, along with the General Staff, that it was the KLA and not Serb forces who were causing the movement of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo. As early as 4 March 1999, prior to the war, General Dimitrijevic specifically reported to the collegiums that intelligence was received -- did I say General Dimitrijevic or General Ojdanic? It was General Dimitrijevic who reported to the collegiums that intelligence was received that very organised activities of the KLA were moving civilians from individual villages to bring the humanitarian crisis to the fore again and provoke a reaction from the international community. That's P933, page 9. The discussion at the collegium of 9 April 1999 is particularly important to understand what General Ojdanic knew about the movement of the population from Kosovo. General Krga, in charge of the intelligence division, described the movement as "the planned withdrawal of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army and the Siptar people from Kosovo and Metohija, which has realistically created a difficult humanitarian situation." Exhibit P929, page 5. Colonel Gajic of the security administration said at the same collegium that "After crushing the terrorist forces of -- in Kosovo, some of them managed, probably in a planned way, to withdraw to Albania, Macedonia, and a few to Montenegro." He predicts that the terrorists will force Albanian and non-Albanian citizens to move out of Kosovo. He goes on to say that "The enemy will conduct planned activity to push out Siptars in order to accuse the army and the state of ethnic cleansing and genocide, thereby creating more favourable grounds for operation by NATO against our forces." That's Exhibit P929, pages 8 to 11. In fact, the discussion at the collegium shows that the staff of the Supreme Command was worried about a ground attack from terrorists mingled with the 400.000 refugees. They proposed announcing publicly that unarmed people and refugees "cannot be played with," and refugees should be allowed to return to their homes. That's at P929, pages 33 and 34 of the 9 April 1999 collegium. That same day, 9 April, General Ojdanic issued a directive which indicated that the army expected infiltration by the KLA on the pretext of securing the return of the refugees, that reception of the refugees on the state border should be organised, that the army should offer assistance to other organs of government for the further care of refugees, that infiltration of the returning refugees by the KLA should be prevented, and that the enemy should be treated in accordance with international humanitarian law. That's P1281. Thus it's clear that as of 9 April 1999, at the level of the staff of the Supreme Command, the displacement of the refugees was believed to have been a KLA tactic to stimulate international support, that it was seen as against the interests of the army and that the return of the refugees was not only contemplated but was to be facilitated. This is hardly consistent with a joint criminal enterprise to deport Kosovo Albanians. Equally inconsistent with such an alleged plan is the announcement made by General Ojdanic on 7 April 1999, the day of the Serbian unilateral cease-fire, encouraging refugees to return to their homes, that announcement set forth in paragraph 263I of our brief. It's noteworthy in his 98 bis argument Mr. Hannis stated concerning the movement of refugees, and this at 12594, Mr. Hannis said, "We're not saying that some of these people didn't leave because of the bombing. We're not saying that some of these people didn't leave their villages because they were told to do so by the KLA in some instances, but we're saying there is evidence upon which you could, as a reasonable trier of fact, find beyond a reasonable doubt that they left because of the violent actions and the force of Serb police and VJ." Let's assume for a moment with Mr. Hannis that the refugee flight was at least due in part to the action of Serb forces. The Prosecution's burden here of course is to further show that these expulsions were the result of a plan, a joint criminal enterprise to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo, and there's nothing in this pre-war conduct of General Ojdanic, we submit, that gives any indication whatever of an intent to join a criminal enterprise to expel Kosovar Albanians. General Ojdanic knew at least as early as 1997, as his comments at the collegium reveal, that the shortest and fastest way to lose Kosovo was by war. As he said in the collegium of 29 June 1998, P927, "I personally still see diplomacy and politics as the only the way out, and I am firmly convinced of that as a soldier. It is utopia for anyone to think that the world will allow us to solve the problems of Kosovo and Metohija by force." And along these same lines in the collegium of 10 April 1998, when he was the deputy chief of staff, General Ojdanic made these very thoughtful, insightful and remarkably prescient comments, that's at 3D657, page 1 and 2, and if the usher would please put that slide up. Showing that even old guys can make one concession to the twenty-first century. We can use this kind of stuff too. It will be the only example we will have in the case. Mr. Visnjic had to teach me how to use it. And in looking at these, what we are -- these are very significant comments in our view, and I would ask you to consider these comments in the context of Judge Bonomy's question to Ms. Kravetz on Tuesday. Did they seriously think they could defeat NATO and clear the country of Albanians? Are the words that we're going to look at now really the words of a person who had in mind going to war and expelling Kosovar Albanians under the cover of NATO bombing? Are these words that follow now the words of General Ojdanic someone who feels that way, that they want to use war as an instrument of policy to effectuate a joint criminal enterprise? And here are the words of General Ojdanic: "General, sir, I will not -- I, General, sir, will not go into international community politics. I will give an assessment from my point of view, and that is what the FRY/Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will not preserve Kosovo by fighting a war. We must look for political and diplomatic solutions. Otherwise, we shall, both as a people and as a state, dive headfirst into calamity. "I would like to present a possible minor subvariant of the possible developments in Kosovo corresponding to the need of our engagement. I think that in the future the Albanians shall continue applying pressure through terrorist activities because that has yielded results so far. Such activities will gradually increase, the aim being for them to become so strong that they cannot objectively be opposed by the MUP/Ministry of the Interior forces as the only competent and internationally recognised force for confronting terrorist groups. "Such I would say an imposed situation would in my opinion be perfidious and its goal would be to force the FRY/Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to engage the VJ/Yugoslav army to destroy the terrorist groups. Such a decision of the FRY would give the Albanians the right to ..." Something happened on my screen. This is why we don't use that technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the problem when old guys use technology, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "Such a decision of the FRY would give the Albanians the right to oppose the VJ and the MUP forces with all their might. Practically speaking, while this would constitute an armed insurrection from our point of view, it would not constitute one in the eyes of the international community. This way, they would all but legalise the armed rebellion. "I am convinced that should we engage in such activity, the international community will not quietly stand aside and watch but will do everything to protect the Albanians in order to address all this at the roundtable, in spite of everything we will have to go through and survive. As far as the Yugoslav army is concerned, General, I think that a decision to engage the Yugoslav army to fight against the terrorist groups would be a big and a difficult one. We know how many of them there are and how strong they are, and we also know which tactics need to be applied to destroy them and the size of the forces needed to truly destroy them. Involving the Yugoslav army on the destruction -- in the destruction of the terrorist groups would practically condemn it. That would mean war." Again, comments made on 10 April 1998 when General Ojdanic was the deputy chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do these comments fit with what actually happened in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, what happened, Your Honour, is that -- that's why I think this is such a prescient comment on the part of General Ojdanic because the KLA activities were increasing because they essentially had reoccupied all of the areas starting with the General Perisic directive of July 1998, it was felt necessary that there had to be some use of the VJ. Again, General Ojdanic saw this as a potential disaster, but because the MUP could not handle it on their own the VJ had to be brought in to take care of the situation. Even Colonel Crosland admitted that. And the continual escalation by the -- by the KLA is what caused the continuing revving up of this operation. That's why I say it was such a prescient comment. I mean, here was July of -- here he's making these comments in April of 1998, and everything he said came true. Very prophetic comments. Knowing therefore that a war over Kosovo was futile and unwinnable, General Ojdanic did his very best to make sure that war never happened as indicated by his continual anti-war comments in the collegiums, his belief in the limited and restrained use of the army, lest [Realtime transcript read in error "less"] it lead to war and his cooperation with the KVM, lest [Realtime transcript read in error "less"] non-cooperation would lead to NATO bombing and war. And it's our further submission that the evidence of General Ojdanic's pre-war conduct was geared solely to dealing with the dual threats of the KLA and NATO, whether the issue was the arming of civilians, the promulgation of war plans, or the troop build-up in the spring of 1999. At the least, General Ojdanic's conduct throughout the pre-war period is consistent with innocence. The Prosecution's conclusion that General Ojdanic joined a criminal enterprise to deport Kosovar Albanians is not the only reasonable conclusion available from the evidence. Now, we spent the first 100 pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There's several times Mr. Sepenuk has used the word "lest" and it appears in the transcript repeatedly as "less." I'm looking at page 24, lines 11 through 13. And a couple of times now his use of the word "lest" has come across as "less" and it does change the meaning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example. Sorry. Page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 24 between lines 11 and 13 he used the worth "lest" twice and it's recorded as "less" and it could be quite confusing when you go back to read what he actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure that will be corrected when the transcript is reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, also page 1, line 14, same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've spent the first 100 pages of our brief discussing the OTP's lack of circumstantial evidence to prove that there was any plan to expel the Kosovar Albanians both before the war and during the war. As set forth in our brief, every member of the General Staff who testified at this trial categorically denied that such a plan ever existed. The best Mr. Hannis could do is to suggest in his oral argument yesterday that all these officers had a motive to lie or kept in the dark about the plan. Your Honours of course are the ultimate judges of a witness's credibility and we presumably won't know your views on this until a judgement is entered. As an aside, however, and for what it's worth, and I hope it's worth something, I note that the only officer of the General Staff whose credibility was seriously questioned at all as I recall was not by the OTP but, rather, by Judge Bonomy, and I refer the Trial Chamber to Judge Bonomy's colloquy with General Obradovic, the assistant Chief of Operations to the General Staff that took place on 6 September 2007, transcript 15162 to 165. There is no time to cite this quite lengthy colloquy except to say that there was mounting frustration on Judge Bonomy's part because General Obradovic, in the view of Judge Bonomy, was repeatedly avoiding answering Judge Bonomy's questions. This matter was resolved by the fortunate intervention of Judge Kamenova at transcript 15164. The transcript simply says: "Trial Chamber confers." Mr. Visnjic and I well remember Judge Bonomy's conferring with Judge Kamenova as if it was yesterday because we, Mr. Visnjic and I, were also frustrated by what appeared to be, what appeared to be General Obradovic's refusal to give a straight answer to Judge Bonomy's question. Judge Kamenova, who understands the Serbian language, no doubt informed Judge Bonomy that it was an error in translation of a document that was creating the difficulty, and there was the English, there was the Serbian, and it just so happened that none of my distinguished Serbian colleagues caught this error, but Judge Kamenova did. And I note this incident, I have to say I'm noting this incident not only to show the lack of any cross-examination by Mr. Hannis and Mr. Stamp trying to show that these -- all these officers lied or were kept in the dark about a plan. There was none of that in this case. But I note this incident also to show how easy it is to get it wrong. Had Judge Kamenova not interjected at that point I think it would have been fair to say that you could -- because you were ready to go on to other subject. You were quite frustrated, as we were, Your Honour, with the witness's answer. Judge Kamenova said, no, it's just a mistake of translation, no problem here. And Your Honour Judge Bonomy, you eventually agreed with that. But I cite it to show how easy it is again to get a wrong, that we'd better pause before we jump to conclusions, as the OTP has done in this case continually and repeatedly in its judgements, its erroneous judgements about General Ojdanic. In any event, as I stated, every member of the General Staff who testified at this trial categorically denied that a plan to deport Kosovar Albanians ever existed, nor was such a plan revealed by the numerous documents that the Ojdanic Defence has presented here. Not selectively but virtually in their entirety, including the collegiums of the General Staff, the General Staff daily briefings, 3rd Army combat reports, Supreme Staff, command staff combat reports and the security administration reports, all of which are attached as annexes in our brief. There's simply no evidence from any witness or document that General Ojdanic ever agreed to, had knowledge of or participated in or aided and abetted any criminal enterprise or operation which had as its objective the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo. The Prosecution has not proven its case against General Ojdanic for individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the statute, and we submit he should be acquitted of these charges. Before discussing the question of General Ojdanic's command responsibility, I want to briefly reply to Mr. Stamp's comments about Dr. Ball and Dr. Fruits. I heard a critique of Dr. Fruits' alleged lack of expertise but nothing about Dr. Ball's built-in bias and lack of objectivity, no better shown than by his comments to the "Cult of the Dead Cow" activist group at their convention in Las Vegas when he said "it would be very nice if we had a round of applause for the extradition of Slobodan Milosevic to The Hague." The transcript says applause. "And I hope you're all as excited as I am by the prospect of his very pleasant and drawn-out trial which will begin in about six months." That's at transcript 10273. Dr. Ball conceded that he had no data in his report on the activities of Serb forces. That fact alone, according to Dr. Fruits, eliminated the possibility of concluding from a statistical standpoint that Serb forces were responsible for migrations and deaths in Kosovo. I've heard nothing from the Prosecution to counter this testimony from Dr. Fruits. As Dr. Fruits also testified, there were flaws in the data concerning KLA attacks and NATO air-strikes. For example, Dr. Fruits noted that there were at least ten NATO air-strikes on 3, 4 April 1999, whereas Dr. Ball's data indicated only two NATO air-strikes on those dates. Dr. Fruits' data highlighted six days where air-strikes occurred, whereas Dr. Ball's data records no air-strikes. I've heard nothing from the Prosecution to counter this testimony of Dr. Fruits. Mr. Stamp also criticises Dr. Fruits for failing to use his data to run further statistical tests. Dr. Fruits was retained jointly by the Defence to show that Dr. Ball's report lacked statistical credibility. In our view he has done precisely that. It was not Dr. Fruits's role to attempt to resuscitate the OTP case. When asked that same question at the trial about doing further statistical steps, Dr. Fruits replied, and this is at 26021, he said: "A. Well, the main reason I didn't do it was because it wasn't my assignment. Another reason is that his data was incorrect, and a third reason is that Dr. Ball et al did not provide sufficient detail of what data they used to produce figure 2 for me to actually perform that analysis." And we'd also refer the Trial Chamber to section 11.1 of Dr. Fruits' report, 3D893 on this point. The Prosecution's criticisms of Dr. Fruits are misplaced. His evidence demonstrates that Dr. Ball's evidence is unreliable and inappropriate in a criminal trial such as this. I'd like to turn now from the pre-war setting to discuss General Ojdanic's wartime conduct and his command responsibility as VJ chief of staff during the 78 days of war. Before analysing the command responsibility of General Ojdanic in regards to VJ forces, it's our submission that MUP forces were not subordinated to the VJ during the war in Kosovo. This is effectively conceded by the Prosecution in its final brief as they do not indicate at any point that subordination occurred. Instead, the OTP adopts a new position stating that, this is in paragraph 246, "Once the state of war was declared on 24 March 1999, the MUP did not submit to full subordination to the VJ for combat operations. Rather, MUP units engaged in joint combat actions on the basis of Joint Command decisions." That General Ojdanic did not have effective control of the MUP is covered very extensively in our brief at paragraphs 454 to 478. This lack of effective control of the MUP also holds true for any crimes that may have been committed by paramilitaries in Kosovo since paramilitaries were not subordinated to VJ forces. While the OTP in paragraph 110 of its brief states that "MUP units were supplemented with paramilitary formations," notably absent is any indication of a link between paramilitary forces and the VJ. It should also be noted that information relating to any specific crimes which are alleged to have been committed by MUP forces did not reach General Ojdanic or the General Staff. Any MUP crimes which may have occurred were required to be reported up the Ministry of Interior chain of command which represented an entirely independent reporting system to that of the VJ. In his military expert report, 3D1116 at paragraph 134, page 121, General Radinovic states that following his examination of all relevant documentary evidence, no MUP war crimes were ever reported to the VJ General Staff. The letter allegedly sent by General Pavkovic to the General Staff on 25 May 1999, which reported serious crimes committed by MUP forces, was never received by General Ojdanic or any member of the General Staff. Further details concerning the authenticity of this letter, P1459, is contained in paragraphs 242 to 249 of our final brief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I've been told I've been speaking too quickly. I apologise and I will slow down accordingly. Now returning to the matter of General Ojdanic's command responsibility over VJ forces. The threshold question that must be satisfied is the establishment of a superior-subordinate relationship. The minimum requirement for recognition of the superior-subordinate relationship is the superior's ability to exercise effective control over the subordinates, meaning "the material ability to prevent or punish" the subordinates' offences. It is axiomatic, therefore, that General Ojdanic would not have had the material ability to prevent or punish criminal conduct of which he was not aware. What is the evidence that General Ojdanic knew of the commission of any of the specific crimes charged in the indictment, and the answer is none. You heard from General Vasiljevic that it was the regular practice for brigades to submit daily combat reports to the Pristina Corps command. The corps command condensed the information into a single report which was forwarded to the 3rd Army. The 3rd Army would condense the reports from the corps and send it on to the Supreme Command Staff. There's no evidence that any of the crimes charged in the indictment were included in any of the daily reports received by General Ojdanic or the Supreme Command Staff. There is no evidence that any of the crimes, nor is there any testimony -- I got a little bit confused there. I apologise. Nor is there any testimony from anyone that they had brought any of the specific crimes listed in the indictment to General Ojdanic's attention. This is confirmed by the military expert General Radinovic who stated in his report that the 3rd Army combat reports contain no data about a single crime alleged in the indictment. That's 3D1116, paragraph 330, page 202. Of course the fact that General Ojdanic did not receive reports of any crimes listed in the indictment does not end our inquiry. General Ojdanic could still be held liable under Article 7(3) if he knew or had reason to know that a crime was about to be or had been committed by a subordinate and he failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crime or punish the perpetrator. I'll turn first to the OTP's claim that General Ojdanic knew or had reason to know that a crime was about to be or had been committed by a subordinate, and here I'm going to do the same thing pretty much that Mr. Fila was talking about yesterday, paragraph by paragraph. It's going to take a bit of time, but the OTP has it so wrong in its brief that there's no way we can -- we can pass it by. We have to let the Court know all of these facts. The OTP's first claim in this regard is that "Ojdanic was aware that thousands of Kosovo Albanians were being forcibly expelled from Kosovo." That's at paragraph 791. Of course the important phrase here is "forcibly expelled," and there is nothing in the bullet points offered by the OTP which points to any such knowledge of General Ojdanic. In its brief the OTP refers to a Supreme Command Staff briefing of 3 April 1999 where General Krga reported the "NATO claim that there are about 500.000 refugees," and suggested that refugee check-points be set up. In response states the OTP brief at paragraph 791, "Ojdanic simply said prepare denials on refugees." Leaving the totally erroneous impression that General Ojdanic was cavalierly denying the existence of a refugee problem. Another instance where the OTP tells only a misleading snippet of the story which I'll now explain. The Supreme Command Staff briefing referred to by the OTP took place on 3 April 1999 starting at 2330 hours, 3D721. Just a half hour before that at 2000 hours General Krga had submitted an intelligence briefing to the General Staff, 3D911, which reported that an American representative had stated that a protectorate "should be established along the border with Albania to monitor the return of Siptars Albanians to the area." 3D911 page 1. General Krga's intelligence report went on to say that "The necessity of establishing a protectorate in Kosovo-Metohija is also being mentioned more and more often in the Western media in the context of the return of refugees and the necessity of their protection." 3D911 page 1. Krga's report concluded with the proposal that "In order to avoid being demonised in the media, I propose that our border organs organise points for the reception of Siptar refugees who are returning to Kosovo Metohija and this should be reported in the media." It was in this context that General Ojdanic's statement "prepare denial on refugees" was issued. This statement followed General Krga's proposal at the General Staff briefing that "refugee check-points be set up" to monitor the return of refugees without external assistance. On this issue the OTP also inexplicably fails to refer to the testimony of Colonel Milovan Novakovic who was a member of the General Staff in charge of information and morale to whose office General Ojdanic referred this task concerning "prepare denial on refugees," as stated in the briefing at 3D721, item 2. In answering a specific question from Mr. Hannis on the phrase used by General Ojdanic, Colonel Novakovic testified: "We were not denying the fact that there were Albania refugees." That's at transcript 16269, 70. Colonel Novakovic went on to say that the General Staff was concerned at the varying and inflated numbers being publicised by NATO. As Colonel Novakovic testified, "That is why we thought and that is why it was up to the position of the collegium that somebody should speak up and say what the truth would be in approximate terms in terms of actual figures." There's no question that General Ojdanic and the General Staff continually acknowledged the importance and significance of the refugee problem. Indeed the OTP itself refers to a Supreme Command Staff briefing on 12 May 1999, where General Krga "reported that the problem of refugees was being stressed in all conferences." That appears at paragraph 791 of the OTP brief. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, is there any evidence of -- of what was said or issued in response to the instruction "prepare denial on refugees"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I wish there was but I do not believe so. Again on the subject of General Ojdanic's alleged knowledge of forceable expulsion of refugees, the OTP in paragraph 791 states: "A Pristina Corps combat report dated 31 March 1999 states that the MUP and the VTOs were channelling Siptar refugees to the Republic of Albania." In support of this claim, the OTP simply refers to Exhibit P2930, item 4, a Pristina Corps command group report which states that "Siptar refugees" are being channelled to the Republic of Albania. What the OTP fails to mention is that this report was sent from the Pristina Corps command group to the Pristina Corps operations centre. It was not routed to the General staff, and therefore General Ojdanic never saw it. So much for the question of his knowledge. However, even if he had seen this document at the relevant time, it would not have been alarming. The reason that these refugees were "channelled" was to ensure only one thing, their safety. Goran Jevtovic, the VJ member who drafted the report in question, that's Exhibit P2930, states that this particular area was ringed by mines and obstacles along with units in combat disposition, and it was necessary for the safety of the civilians to channel or direct them in safe directions. That's 5D1385, paragraph 22. This protection of the welfare of civilians where there were mines in the area is corroborated by the testimony of Delic 19306-7, and Halimi 4492. In short, as further evidence of the weakness of their case, the OTP has improperly taken this snippet, this little bit of a report out of the context of a true situation to impute to General Ojdanic a knowledge he never had. Having failed to establish General Ojdanic's knowledge that Kosovar Albanians were being forcibly expelled, the OTP turns to its next allegation that "Ojdanic was aware of other crimes against Kosovo Albanians." That's paragraph 792. The OTP then sets forth some eight examples concerning General Ojdanic's knowledge of crimes and concludes in paragraph 793 that despite his awareness of these crimes Ojdanic "took no concrete action." We'll examine each of these eight incidents in turn to show that they are both baseless and misleading. The OTP first claims that on -- that "on 3 April 1999, during a Supreme Court staff briefing, Krga reported problems with looting and that 32 volunteers of the 175th Infantry Brigade had been sent back." In fact, it was Colonel Gajic who made this report, not Krga. As noted by this exhibit 3D721, those volunteers were sent back from Kosovo. In this same General Staff briefing of 3 April 1999, General Ojdanic responds to this incident of looting by volunteers by stating, "The command of the 3rd Army is to explain why these 32 were together and not in the units." That's 3D721, page 2. Dividing the volunteers and not allowing them to serve in the VJ as a group would have been in compliance with General Ojdanic's orders regarding the admission of volunteers as more fully explained in our brief at paragraphs 269 to 271. In addition, the Gajic testimony cited but not explained by the OTP, 15332-33 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down once again, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I hope this is the last time I've been warned about slowing down. I'll really try to keep it very measured. I apologise for that. In any event, the Gajic testimony confirms that these men who committed crimes were arrested and convicted while the remainder of -- while the remainder of the unit was removed from Kosovo-Metohija. So much for the baseless and rather startling OTP claim in paragraph 793 that "Ojdanic took no concrete action." The next example cited by the OTP is that, "On 5 April 1999, during the supreme -- the SC staff briefing, Colonel Gajic reported that "bands stealing from the local population had appeared in Kosovo." This is by no means a specific allegation that could realistically be processed or prosecuted. Further, the word "bands" does not indicate that this was VJ forces, MUP, paramilitaries or rogue civilians acting on their own, aside from the fact that a military justice system had been established by General Ojdanic and the VJ for the arrest of any crime perpetrators. The next OTP claim is that, "In April 1999, security organs of the Pristina Corps received a report from the MUP on the execution of 20 civilians in Mali Alas in April 1999, allegedly by the 252nd Armoured Brigade. The chief of the security of the Pristina Corps reported this to Vasiljevic." What the OTP fails to mention is that Vasiljevic did not find out about the murder of these civilians until early May 1999 when he was in Kosovo, as his statement makes clear. Neither Vasiljevic nor Ojdanic knew about this at the time. Also not mentioned by the OTP is that this case was transferred to a civilian court. This is explained in the testimony -- in the testimony of the witness Mladenovic who stated that following an investigation by the military prosecutor it was determined that no military personnel had been involved in the murders but, rather, civilians from that area. 21260-261. The next OTP claim is that "On 18 April 1999, during the Supreme Command staff briefing Gajic reported a rape case from the 52nd Air Defence Artillery and Rocket Brigade and looting in the Djakovica area." This precise case is dealt with in paragraph 261 of our brief, and the short of it is that the soldiers committing the rape were identified, arrested, a criminal report was filed, and as far as Colonel Gajic knew, the perpetrators were convicted and sentenced to prison. So much again for the OTP claim that General Ojdanic took no concrete action as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On this occasion, though, that's recognised in the OTP brief. The footnote makes it sure that there was a prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's -- I'm glad it was clear to Your Honour, I am, but the way it was presented by the OTP, quite frankly, Your Honour, I didn't think it was that clear. It was footnoted. I think it should have been in the text. The next OTP claim is that "On 26 April 1999, or thereabouts, the Supreme Command Staff received a Pristina Corps request for the engagement of a forensic pathologist to exhume bodies buried in graves in Kosovo. Lazarevic reported that "There are indications that members of the army are responsible." All we can say to this is that a forensic examiner being sent to exhume bodies necessarily negates the idea of some plot to cover up the deaths. This was a good faith effort of the VJ to determine if members of the army were in fact responsible. The next OTP claim is as follows: "In early May 1999, the VJ security administration was informed that crimes were being committed in Kosovo and that volunteer groups were present there. Farkas inspected the security organs in Kosovo between 5-6 May 1999, and upon returning reported to Ojdanic that crimes were being committed in Kosovo and were not reported up to the Supreme Command Staff. There were rapes, looting, and theft." Of course what the OTP fails to mention is that Farkas was sent to Kosovo by General Ojdanic in early May specifically to investigate problems of which he had just become aware. The evidence is clear that General Ojdanic reacted strongly upon hearing that crimes were not being reported and proactive measures were taken to uncover further crimes during the next few weeks including meetings with General Pavkovic, President Milosevic and others. This issue is addressed in paragraphs 334 to 352 of our brief. The next OTP claim is that "On 6 May 1999, the Supreme Court staff intelligence department reported that General Clark 'assessed that there was no longer a possibility for the VJ to continue with ethnic cleansing in Kosovo.'" It's difficult to understand what the OTP is driving at here. Surely General Clark, indeed the enemy at this point in May 1999, can hardly be cited as any kind of dispassionate observer on whether there was knowledge on the part of General Ojdanic or the General Staff of the forcible expulsion of Kosovar Albanians. This is particularly true since after two years of trial, the best that the OTP can do on this issue is the evidence contained in paragraph 791 of its brief, which I hope we have shown is without merit. The last OTP allegation in this regard is that "On 8 May 1999, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Djurovic, the deputy of the Pristina Corps security, met with Vasiljevic in Belgrade and informed him about the crimes against civilians committed by the military. These included a rape case and two murders. Vasiljevic instructed him to prepare a report." This set of facts is covered in our brief at paragraph 339 as part of the section of our brief in which General Ojdanic begins to receive a flow of information in May 1999 regarding some unreported crimes and is proactive concerned measures to remedy any reporting deficiencies. Vasiljevic stated that his impression was that this was the first time General Ojdanic had heard about these crimes. The fact is as set forth extensively in our brief that General Ojdanic did not receive complete information regarding VJ activity in the field in Kosovo. More specifically, General Ojdanic did not have knowledge of widespread crimes committed or about to be committed sufficient to declare either actual or inquiry notice. This lack of knowledge in regards to crimes allegedly committed by VJ forces is described in detail in paragraphs 252 -- 256 to 262 of our final brief. For instance, Generals Curcin and Simic and Colonel Ivkovic, among others in the VJ General Staff, testified that the Supreme Command Staff did not have knowledge of massive violations of international humanitarian law but, rather, only received information indicating isolated and unorganised criminal behaviour, unorganised criminal behaviour, on behalf of individual soldiers that were being successfully resolved. 3D1121, paragraph 27. 3D1089, page 11. 3D1117, paragraph 13 and 27 respectively. The texts of all collegiums, Supreme Command combat reports, daily briefings, security administration reports and 3rd Army reports are attached as annexes to our brief. A careful examination of the abundance of documentary evidence fails to locate any instance which would have provided General Ojdanic with knowledge or a reason to know that massive crimes against humanity were occurring in Kosovo. Rather, similar to the testimony you've heard, through the testimony that you've heard, a review of the Pristina Corps and 3rd Army combat reports indicated that the staff of the Supreme Command was being informed in general of the commission of some crimes in Kosovo and was being consistently assured that these crimes were being adequately addressed by the military justice organs. On the subject of reporting on widespread crimes I want to take a brief detour here to take some issue with paragraph 221 of General Pavkovic's brief. This paragraph refers to an article from the Politika newspaper of 5 May 1999, which is Exhibit 4D406. This article reports the commission of numerous serious crimes within Kosovo, the arrest of several hundred perpetrators, and the imposition of a large number of sentences from 5 to 20 years' imprisonment for these crimes as that paragraph in the Pavkovic brief states. The Ojdanic Defence, in a written submission of 15 November 2007, objected on several grounds to the admission of this newspaper article from the bar table when it was first offered into evidence. Among other objections to its unreliability as a newspaper article, the Ojdanic Defence pointed out that the best evidence of reporting of war crimes were the combat reports of the 3rd Army and that the article's contents had already been refuted by the testimony of General Radomir Gojevic, the chief legal officer of the General Staff, particularly to the extent that it reported massive war crimes followed by lengthy prison sentences. In its decision of 28 November 2007, the Trial Chamber ruled in paragraph 6 that 4D406, as was generally the case with newspaper articles, was not admissible to prove the truth of its contents. So we submit that paragraph 221 of the Pavkovic brief should not be given any weight by the Trial Chamber. I should add that while this article is not admissible to prove the truth of its contents, the Trial Chamber may recall that the Ojdanic Defence had no objection to the admissibility of this article simply to show knowledge of its contents when it was sent to certain recipients in the MUP to take measures against the commission of crimes. This is reflected in the testimony of the witness Mijatovic at TR22547-549. Judge Bonomy pointed out at that time the distinction between excluding this document as to the truth of its contents but admitting it solely on the issue of notice. Returning to the subject as to when General Ojdanic became aware of unreported crimes, General Vasiljevic testified that General Ojdanic sent him and General Gajic to Kosovo to gather more detailed information about what was going on concerning crimes, looting, and the other problems that were reported. General Vasiljevic learned during this investigation that there had been a decision by the army command in Pristina not to report the commission of some crimes to the Supreme Command Staff. General Vasiljevic went on to say that the 3rd Army had investigated and processed these cases and therefore they thought it unnecessary to further report these particular cases up the chain of command. This is transcript 8647, 8651. I'd like to pause briefly here to consider the OTP claim about General Ojdanic's failure to discipline or discharge General Pavkovic for his conduct both before and during the war. The OTP first claims that Pavkovic sent inaccurate reports to the General Staff by stating that it was the KLA and not Serb forces who were primarily -- who were primarily responsible for provocations before the war. We've already dealt with this issue by pointing out inter alia that there was no specific information other than an assertion by General Dimitrijevic that these reports were inaccurate, and Dimitrijevic testified that when General Ojdanic said he would be meeting with General Pavkovic about this, he had no reason to doubt that since General Ojdanic usually followed through on what he had to say -- on what he had said. The OTP next claims that the 3rd Army command failed to report crimes to the General Staff during the war. However, as shown by the testimony of General Vasiljevic, these crimes, though not reported to the General Staff, were in fact processed and prosecuted by the responsible lower commands. This bottleneck, therefore, can be described more accurately as an inadvertent lack of communication as opposed to any wilful attempt to misinform, and this circumstance is covered in our final brief at paragraphs 250 to 255. The short of it is that there was no compelling reason to suspend or discipline the commander of the 3rd Army in the midst of a NATO bombing campaign and the separatist and violent actions of the KLA. We suggest that it would have been ill-advised and irresponsible to change commanders in the middle of the war under these circumstances, despite the urgings of General Hannis and General Stamp to substitute their judgement for that of General Ojdanic. All this is aside from the fact that General Ojdanic did hold General Pavkovic accountable by calling him to Belgrade in mid-May 1999 after General Ojdanic was informed of the indication of widespread crimes by Generals Farkas and Vasiljevic. General Pavkovic made his explanations to Mr. Milosevic and others at this Belgrade meeting. General Ojdanic then took steps to further investigate by sending his own officers, Vasiljevic and Gajic, to the field. The efforts of Vasiljevic and Gajic to investigate and discover other crimes is set forth in paragraphs 363 to 375 of our brief. In addition, there were further efforts to discover crimes which were directed by General Ojdanic. This included, for instance, seven wartime tours in Kosovo on behalf of the General Staff, as well as some 83 inspections at the brigade and battalion level. And this is all set forth in 3D1116, page 171, 3D1115, paragraph 20. It's significant to mention at this point that General Simic testified that these inspections did not result in any indication to the General Staff that war crimes were being committed on the ground by VJ forces. 3D1089 and 3D489. Another important example of General Ojdanic's efforts can be seen following his receipt of the Louise Arbour letter on 2 -- May 29, 1999. General Ojdanic forwarded this letter to the legal administration requesting that a draft order to prevent war crimes and punish perpetrators. The end result was an order which stated "each military officer who knows of the perpetration of violations of the principles, rules and regulations of international war law who does not initiate disciplinary or criminal procedure shall be personally responsible." 3D483. This example and many others show that General Ojdanic met the last requirement under Article 7(3), that he took the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crime or punish the perpetrators, and details of this appear in our final brief at paragraphs 516 to 534. As an example, during the war General Ojdanic issued some 18 good faith orders directed at compliance with the international laws of war. Most of these orders are set forth in our brief, and they are all listed in General Radinovic's military expert report 3D116 paragraphs 153, 154. Additionally, issues related to the observance of humanitarian law were regularly discussed in the daily briefings of the General Staff. These briefings are summarised in the military expert report of General Radinovic at 3D1116, pages 155 to 157. That might be paragraphs. I'm not clear on that. It's either pages or paragraphs. I wonder, Your Honours, if this might be an appropriate -- I'm going on to another subject now which will take a few minutes of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I would say no, Your Honour. I would say 10 -- 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I would apologise asking you something at the very beginning instead of disturbing you and spoiling your eloquence. Now, on page 44, line 2, what I read it as that the lower command did not report things, but what is -- what is attributed to them is inadvertence and not anything purposeful, and then we also find that the communication -- there were bottlenecks in communication and the general did not receive it. Now, what can this be due to, lack of leadership or something purposeful where -- where things have been suppressed? If it is inadvertent, it is very strange. And how can it be inadvertence in a disciplined force like the army? And then we find Louise Arbour talking of certain things and communicating it, and of course he took action, as you said. But these are paradoxes which have bothered me, and I thought that it's good that I made a request to you to kindly clear it up so that I acknowledge things in the right way. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, in good part following the testimony of General Vasiljevic who said that in his opinion he thought it was inadvertent, that the crimes were being processed and prosecuted in the lower units and therefore the decision was made that it wasn't really necessary to report the crimes up the line, and he was satisfied that the crimes were indeed being prosecuted and I go into that a little bit further in the last part of my argument. Yes, it could be a lack of leadership. It could be a lack of control. I don't think -- you know, it should have been reported up. We don't deny that at all. But I don't think there was any -- certainly no criminal intent here or even criminal negligence. Indeed be criminal negligence if the crimes were reported and not punished. That would indeed be criminal. But the failure to report the crimes in our view was inadvertent. Now, again it may have been a failure of leadership but I would say nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But wasn't there an intelligence system reporting to the chief of army staff about all these happenings? When somebody in a remote place, I mean so remotely away like at The Hague and the knowledge of it and things are being formulated by him and reported and then action is taken. Now, this I was not able to reconcile, and I seek your help and what have you to say to help me in this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, of course yes, there was and intelligence system through the intelligence division and dealing mostly with the KLA and NATO, and then course there was the security administration dealing with the report of crimes and what not, but again I'm -- I wish I could do better and to explain the so-called bottleneck, but again to me, at least to the Ojdanic Defence, the bottom line is that these crimes were reported ultimately and prosecuted. Is that satisfactory, Judge Chowhan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm very grateful that you responded to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What the Honourable Judge was telling me was that you did understand me when I said Louise Arbour. That's the Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, sure. Louise Arbour, correct, absolutely, yes. We were dealing with attempting to show that General Ojdanic met the last requirement under Article 7(3), that he took the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crime and to punish the perpetrators. We just talked about the number of orders that he issued directed at compliance with the international laws of war. The OTP in paragraph 825 of its brief claims that the distribution of some 1.300 copies of the rules of combatants for combatants was "clearly insufficient" to meet the needs of the 14.000 soldiers of the Pristina Corps. This statement is based on a misreading of the record by the OTP which I'd now like to clarify. The Trial Chamber will recall the small four-page laminated pamphlet 3D988 entitled "rules of conduct for soldiers," which briefly and clearly summarises a soldier's duty to treat both combatants and civilians humanely. I'm sure you all remember that little laminated pamphlet that fits in your wallet or inside pocket. Both General Gojevic, the chief legal officer of the army General Staff, and General Farkas, the chief of VJ security, testified that this leaflet was distributed to every soldier in the army at the beginning of the war. That's Gojevic at 16647-48 and Farkas at 16315. The OTP conveniently overlooks this testimony and states at paragraphs 824, 825 of its brief that only 350 copies of this pamphlet was distributed to soldiers in the Pristina Corps. We suggest that the OTP has gotten it wrong here again, but I think in fairness to the OTP that the OTP might have been inadvertently misled by material contained in the Radinovic report at paragraphs 186 to 190. That expert report does state at paragraph 189 that 350 of these pamphlets from a larger group of some 1.300 copies were distributed to soldiers in the 3rd Army. In fact, what apparently was distributed, as indicated by the statement of Ojdanic Defence witness General Gajic, that's 3D1084 at paragraph 145, was "1.300 copies of the International Red Cross brochure" which cited various obligations of combatants to observe international humanitarian law. That's at 15277. In any event the testimony of Generals Gojevic and Farkas that every soldier received a copy of the rules of conduct was reaffirmed by General Radinovic in his expert report. If the OTP had just read a bit further down the page, General Radinovic states, "Moreover, such short and succinct formulations are amenable to printing in pocket format which too made it possible for the rules to be found in the pocket of every VJ member in Kosovo and Metohija." That's 3D1116, paragraph 191. It's really clear that every VJ soldier received a copy of this pamphlet. Just as General Ojdanic fulfilled his duty to prevent crimes, so did he did ensure that all reasonable and necessary measures were taken to prosecute and punish criminal offenders.
