A matter of hours after NATO air-strikes had commenced on the evening of 24 March 1999, General Ojdanic ordered that all wartime military courts and wartime military prosecutors be mobilised and that they organise their work immediately. In under one week's time, the chief of the legal section of the General Staff had inspected and visited wartime judicial organs in the 3rd Army and determined that they were "ready with regard to personnel and expertise to carry out tasks within their competence." 3D804, paragraph 3.3. As an example of the diligence -- of his diligence in overseeing the military justice system we call the Trial Chamber's attention to Annex G of our final brief. This annex shows that General Ojdanic received an update on the work of judicial organs on 63 of 78 days during the war. Of course the military justice system had its flaws, but when problems were identified, they were immediately addressed and corrected. General Gojevic, who was in charge of the legal section of the General Staff, testified that on 12 May 1999, he wrote a report to the Supreme Court staff -- to the Supreme Command Staff stating his assessment that "The volume and complexity of the tasked faced by military judicial organs was too great a load for the existing establishment and after making adjustments and overcoming initial difficulties, the military judicial organs have become fully operational." P2826, paragraph 2.3. Further, General Gojevic testified very significantly that he did not know of a single reported war crime that was not investigated and processed through the criminal justice system. 16686. We should note that General Ojdanic himself questioned General Gojevic after the war about the relatively low number of persons prosecuted for serious war crimes. We noted General Gojevic's answer to General Ojdanic in our brief at paragraph 310, and we suggest it's worth repeating because his words make sense. I hope it makes sense to the Trial Chamber. He said, "In times of war it's very difficult to identify perpetrators and find them because the perpetrators hide very well. There is an atmosphere of fear, so that even those in the immediate surroundings of perpetrators are reluctant to report them. And even in cases when only fighting men were concerned, this seemed to be true as well. That is the flip side, the negative side of solidarity, but it's typical of all soldiers that they are bound by ties of solidarity regardless of the circumstances." That's at 16685. As the war drew to a close and as the extent of certain crimes began to come to light at the level of the Supreme Command, a briefing was held by the Supreme Command Staff. According to the notes of this briefing which is Exhibit 3D493, General Farkas reported that a full analysis had been made of the problems involving humanitarian crime. He said that most of the atrocities and serious crimes from looting to rapes had been documented and were now before military court organs. He said that around 95 per cent of the perpetrators had been arrested or were under investigation. At this meeting General Ojdanic issued a document ordering that military judicial organs should prioritise their prosecution of crimes and that violations of international law must be the first priority. That's Exhibit 4D487. Therefore, the evidence in this case shows that General Ojdanic had no knowledge of the specific crimes alleged in the indictment and therefore no ability or duty to prevent or punish them -- or punish them. The evidence also shows that he was affirmatively informed that the movement of the population was the result of either NATO bombing or KLA actions, not that of the army. And the evidence further shows that when he was informed of violations of international humanitarian law being committed by members of the army in Kosovo, he took swift and repeated steps to investigate, prevent, and punish those crimes. A review of the jurisprudence that sets out the standards of a top commander such as General Ojdanic shows that his actions were appropriate and proper. This jurisprudence is fully set forth in our brief and I don't think bears repeating here. I would only reiterate for the Trial Chamber that during the war General Ojdanic was located primarily in a bunker hundreds of feet under the ground in Belgrade and wholly dependent upon the information he received from subordinates. His country was subject to massive air bombardment, mass insurgency and the prospect of imminent land invasion. We ask you to take account of this in judging whether General Ojdanic's actions met the standards of accountability for a top commander as we so strongly urged. To conclude and to step back for a moment to look at the big picture, if General Ojdanic was in fact responsible for the deportation and murder of Albanians, either individually or as a superior commander, don't you think you would have heard some evidence about that? The Prosecution in this case has a good part of the entire international community behind it. It has tremendous evidence-gathering capabilities, not only from NATO and its member countries but from Serbia itself. It has access to the most candid conversations of General Ojdanic, whether it be electronic surveillance, the verbatim transcripts of the General Staff collegiums, or the insiders who have come to testify during this trial, particularly Generals Vasiljevic and Dimitrijevic. It has access to all the orders issued before, during, and after the war, and all of the combat reports. From all of these sources there is no smoking gun, not even a wisp of smoke. There is no evidence against General Ojdanic for one simple reason. He is not guilty. You are all experienced Judges. You know what is fair and you know proof beyond a reasonable doubt when you see it. The Prosecutor's case has fallen short of this standard and it's done so not for lack of effort or for lack of good advocacy. It has fallen short because General Ojdanic is truly not guilty. I suggest that to find General Ojdanic guilty you would have to affirmatively disbelieve Prosecution witness General Vasiljevic who showed how General Ojdanic did all he could to get to the bottom of crimes in Kosovo. The Court's own witness, General Dimitrijevic, who affirmed that General Ojdanic was sincere in his efforts to get accurate information from Kosovo and the numerous officers of the Yugoslavian army who came into this courtroom in person or by videolink and told it as it was. Indeed, it is hard to imagine more exemplary conduct by a military leader during a war. General Ojdanic organised seminars, issued orders, distributed pamphlets, screened volunteers and banned paramilitaries to ensure that the standards of international humanitarian law would be observe. When he learned of problems he ordered investigations, sent personal emissaries, upgraded the military justice system, alerted President Milosevic, advocated the creation of a state investigation commission and made personal pleas to Albanians to remain in their homes, and all for a battle he never sought and a war he never wanted. Mr. Visnjic and I have been privileged to represent General Ojdanic. He's no criminal. He's a good man, a good soldier and a good commander. He is unjustly accused. The events that unfolded in Kosovo in 1999 are tragic indeed, but a rational judgement must declare that General Ojdanic stood for peace and conciliation, not for war and discrimination. He should be acquitted on all counts of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That completes it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're just frightened to move off that seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's my last gasp, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Sepenuk, for these submissions. We will now hear closing arguments on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning and good morning to everyone in this court. To some extent I guess I share the feelings of Mr. Fila about how much can really be accomplished by arguing to you after you have sat there for two years and so carefully listened to what we've been doing here and followed this, and I -- it's been remarkable to me really how diligent you've been in that regard, and I think we're all privileged to have such a good Trial Chamber to try this case to. But you know, I'm an old trial lawyer, and old trial lawyers are like racehorses. You put them in the gate and you open the gate and they're going to run until you tell them to stop, so here I go. We've come to the end of what I think is a long and sometimes dusty and sometimes unmarked road, and I'd probably be remiss, Judge Bonomy, if I didn't also say in the spirit of motions that I've filed one without any speed limit, but here we are. I'm not even going to make an attempt to summarise the two years of testimony and exhibits that we have seen as we've gone through at this time. I think my approach to this argument must be simply one of -- of looking at what the OTP says is their best case and telling you why I believe it is not, and so that's what I'm going to do. On occasion I will go beyond the OTP brief and argument, but rarely, I suppose. You've heard three persons speak in front of me, and I suspect it has come to your attention that all of them were critical of various parts of the Prosecution's brief as being misleading or as not being accurate, and I think that's a bit remarkable for a brief in a case of this nature, and I must say to you that I was stunned a bit when I started looking at the Prosecution's brief and looking at what was said and how the footnotes failed to support many of the things that were said, and I say that with some regret, because I have huge respect for Mr. Hannis and the people who have worked under him throughout this trial, and I don't know how it happened that their brief got in the state that it got into, but it is not what it should be, in my view, and I will spend some time talking to you about that. I say that at the beginning to second the arguments made by my colleagues but also to urge all of you to pay very particular attention to the things that are written in the Prosecutor's brief and make certain that there's evidence that supports them and make certain that what they cite in the footnotes really supports what they say in the paragraphs. You all know that as you consider the evidence in this case that -- that what we expect of you and what the law expects of you, what the tradition of our profession expects of you is that you judge the evidence in this case by the standards that protect the freedom and integrity of the rule of law, and that is you judge it by the standards of holding the Prosecution to their task of proving guilt in this case beyond a reasonable doubt. And you can hear Mr. Hannis tell you that you have to adopt the most likely thing, and you have to use Occam's razor and say, you know, apply that to it, but if -- Mr. Hannis probably would like that to be the law but that's not the law, and you must apply the law and I know you will. You know that when there are two reasonable conclusions you always must adopt the one that's most consistent with the innocence of the person standing before you. There are to me some fairly obvious questions that you should ask as you analyse the evidence in this case. Mr. Stamp spoke to you the first day about witness credibility. Mr. Hannis talked about witness credibility, suggesting that some witnesses had an interest that would make their testimony maybe less than credible. The first thing I want to say about that is we probably couldn't have tried this case at a more unfortunate time, but that's the way the time worked out. We tried the case involving the events in Kosovo right in the middle of the negotiations regarding the independence of Kosovo, so that there were -- there were political considerations on both sides with the witnesses that came in to testify in this case. They had to have in their minds, it seems to me, what effect their testimony might have on the efforts to achieve independence by Kosovo, and I think it's just something to keep perhaps in the back of your minds as you make your way through this evidence. Mr. O'Sullivan talked to you a little bit about this issue, and that is what was it the NATO intervention was really about. It was publicly announced as a -- an action to prevent a humanitarian crisis. I think if anything is clear at this point it is that that is not what it was, that that was merely a pretext for what I say was an effort to change the Milosevic regime. The goal here was regime change, not avoiding a humanitarian crisis. And there's a lot of evidence that supports that. There's the testimony of John Crosland, who said that's what it was about, who knew that's what it was about. And there's the -- the indictment in this case. I think it's interesting, if there was a humanitarian crisis going on, that would have to be a crisis that would involve the commission of crimes, it would seem to me, either deportations or murders or something of that nature, something that would qualify as a humanitarian crisis caused by individuals, people, and yet the first crime that's charged in this indictment is not until the 24th of March, the day that NATO started bombing. So that's when the humanitarian crisis began according to the indictment of the Prosecutor. I -- I have the good fortune in this case to represent General Pavkovic. General Pavkovic is an intelligent, accomplished professional soldier and has been throughout his entire military career. Every step through his career has been exemplary. He was at the top of his class in every course that he took in his career in the army. He was promoted ahead of his colleagues in almost every promotion that he received in his career in the army. His superiors always gave him the highest possible ratings. And all of this is in the evidence in this case. You will remember Shaun Byrnes talking about General Pavkovic. He said he was direct and professional. He referred to him as a soldier's soldier who didn't get involved in lectures on Serb history or politics. He also said that his view of the VJ was that it conducted itself both professionally and honourably both before and during the conflict. Now, that's a VJ that was under the command of General Pavkovic, a general who insisted that those under his command conduct themselves professionally and honourably and would not countenance their failure to do that. And while I'm talking about Shaun Byrnes, let me just mention that -- what he said about the allegations of excessive force. It says his view that shelling that VJ did with their heavy weaponry was not intended to cause casualties but more in the nature of causing harassment or fear, and that is to, I say, warn the civilian population that there may be an action coming up and that they should get out of the way. If I could point you to one thing in this record which I think virtually compels the acquittal of General Pavkovic, it is the evidence about the meetings of the 16th and 17th of May in Belgrade when General Ojdanic asked General Pavkovic to come to Belgrade and talk about some things he'd heard about crimes being committed. Pavkovic came and reported both in a meeting on the 16th with Ojdanic and others and the next day in a meeting with Milosevic, and you will recall that in both of those meetings Pavkovic urged the formation of an investigative commission to look into the matter in depth and make determinations about the commission of crimes, who was responsible for the commission of crimes, and to really get to the bottom of the issue. Now, that is not something that would be done by a person who believes that the result of that investigation would be to implicate him. That's the recommendation of a person who knows that he himself is clear of any accusation about that but that also knows there is something fishy going on down there that somebody ought to take a look at. And I think it's notable that both General Ojdanic, and the next day General Ojdanic and Sainovic agreed with Pavkovic about that and urged Milosevic to do that, and Milosevic didn't, and we don't know why. The only thing we really know was at the end of that meeting Milosevic urged some people to remain after the army personnel had left, and it would be interesting to know what happened in that next meeting. I can assure you this: If General Ojdanic had proposed the formation of such a commission and General Pavkovic had opposed it, that would be some of the strongest evidence the Prosecution could possibly have against him. The other side of that shows you his innocence. You've heard a lot about the -- the Prosecution's theory on the JCE, the plan, the modification of the ethnic balance, the use of NATO bombing as cover for carrying that out, and I'm not going to spend very much time talking about because you've heard all about it already but just suggest to you that the Prosecution hasn't even come close to proving that to you beyond a reasonable doubt. It's argued in our brief. It's argued extremely well in the Ojdanic brief. The Prosecution argued on the first day and they argue in their brief, Ms. Kravetz talked about it and the brief talks about it, and what they say is that the evidence for the existence of this joint criminal enterprise is the crime base that you have heard about, that people left Kosovo, that people were killed, that some rapes occurred, that the fact that those happened throughout Kosovo is evidence that there was a plan. And what I ask you to do is just pick a war. I don't care which one you pick, just pick any one. What happens in wars when bombs are being dropped is people leave and people are killed and rapes happen, and other crimes happen, lootings happen. All these things happen. The fact that Kosovo looked the same as every other war we've ever seen does not prove that there was an overarching joint criminal enterprise plan in Kosovo. It just shows you that it was another war where things happened just like happened in every other war. That's not a pattern that proves JCE. On the second day beginning at page 82 of the transcript, Mr. Hannis went through an exercise where he started with Ojdanic's Grom 3 directive and traced it down through a series of first an order from the 3rd Army and then down through a series of orders from the Pristina Corps to the brigade level and so forth to show you that the -- the actions that were carried out were first ordered at the very top and then carried down through the chain of command and then carried out around the country in accordance with that Grom 3 directive. These are all perfectly legal orders. They were appropriate military actions against terrorists. They don't order the commission of any crimes. They're the kind of orders you'd expect to find in any professional military organisation trying to protect its borders and deal with a terrorist uprising at the same time. They prove no crime charged in this indictment. They're no indication whatsoever of the existence of the JCE as alleged. In his presentation Mr. Hannis made suggestions about possibilities. He raised matters that you should view as suspicious, but this is a criminal case, remember. Allegations must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Suspicions and possibilities are not sufficient for conviction. One thing that you've heard the Prosecution talk about, and you'll find it in their brief, paragraph 696 is one place, when they're trying to use things that happened in 1998 as evidence regarding 1999, one of the arguments is that the powers that be, General Pavkovic and others, should have known in 1999, because of what they learned from 1998, that crimes were going to be committed and should have done something about that, because they say it was the same forces. But first of all you haven't heard one bit of evidence that it was the same forces. In fact, what you've heard is it was not. The people down on the ground doing the fighting were conscripts who were cycling in and out of Kosovo all the time. They'd finish their military obligation and they were gone and new conscripts would come in, and new conscripts were coming in all the time, and that is why you see General Pavkovic over and over sending out orders regarding adherence to the laws of war, because he knew about every 30 days there was a new group of soldiers down there and he wanted to remind his commanders to remind them to adhere to the law. There's been an enormous amount of -- of smoke and argument about the alleged illegal use of the VJ in Kosovo in 1998. It's been talked about throughout this trial. You know what the law is. You've seen the law, and you know that the VJ could have operated legally as it in fact operated in Kosovo in 1998. I think this whole issue about illegal use of the VJ was a smokescreen created by Perisic and his supporters in the General Staff who were expressing their jealousies and who were disgruntled with their loss of power. If Perisic was really concerned that General Pavkovic was somehow using the VJ illegally, he was the commanding General. All he had to do was remove him. He didn't even take the first step to do that. So I think it's all just made up. It all arose out of that letter that Perisic sent to Milosevic and his complaints about the use of the VJ. And one thing that I think has gotten completely befuddled in all of this, and it has even confused some of my colleagues as you may have just heard. Perisic is not saying to Milosevic, "We shouldn't be using the VJ against terrorists in Kosovo," at all. He's not saying that at all. He's saying, "To use the VJ against terrorists in Kosovo we need to declare a state of emergency or state of war. Now, let's do that. Let's declare that state of emergency or state of war because I want to mount a really, really massive campaign against these people." And they wouldn't do that. And there were reasons they wouldn't do that, and General Pavkovic set out those reasons pretty clearly in his October report. They were dealing with a diplomatic situation that simply would not have allowed them to do what Perisic wanted done, and that is declare this state of war or state of emergency. The contention that the army was being used unconstitutionally, we keep hearing that, and I think I distinctly said in my arguments at the 98 bis level, if the Prosecution can find anywhere in the constitution any constitutional provision that was being violated by the use the army, tell us what it is, and that's never happened. And you can read the constitution, Your Honours, until you turn blue and you won't find it, because there's nothing unconstitutional about the way the army was being used. Paragraph 856 of the Prosecutor's brief says: "Samardzic tried to initiate disciplinary proceedings against Pavkovic." You will not find any evidence, direct evidence, in this record that General Pavkovic ever used a Pristina Corps unit except pursuant to an order coming down through the chain of command, not one. There's no evidence beyond the uncorroborated evidence of Dimitrijevic that Samardzic made any efforts to discipline Pavkovic, and I suggest to you Dimitrijevic is simply part of the Perisic cabal that does not like what happened in terms of their loss of power. In the footnote to paragraph 856, the OTP relies on the Samardzic [sic] testimony, and also they say that this is also proved by Exhibit P922, but that exhibit says absolutely nothing about a Samardzic effort to discipline Pavkovic, although they cite it in support of their assertion. 64, line 13 says Samardzic testimony. It should be Dimitrijevic testimony. I suggest to you this whole thing was an invention of Dimitrijevic. You've got to remember that in the assessment of the performance of General Nebojsa Pavkovic from the period 29 June 1997 to 10 January 1999, an assessment written by General Samardzic, who Dimitrijevic tells you tried to initiate disciplinary proceedings against him, he says about General -- General Pavkovic as commander of the 3rd Army, Pristina Corps: "He showed superior qualities that he had been continuously improving on over time as a result of several previously held important posts in the Pristina Corps command and the Main Staff of the Yugoslav army. Owing to such results and related intellectual and moral qualities, General Pavkovic was exceptionally promoted to the rank of lieutenant general. His assessment is positive with the mark exceptional." And I think it was General Vasiljevic who told you that's the highest possible rating that he could have gotten. At paragraph 701 of their brief the OTP makes this argument: "President Djukanovic raised the issue of possible crimes committed in Kosovo." Now, I underline possible crimes. "Raised the issue of possible crimes committed in Kosovo by pointing to information indicating that the Pristina Corps actions were not always in accordance with the constitutional role of the army and the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." And the reference there is to P1000, pages 9 and 10. This concern expressed by Djukanovic does not raise the issue of possible crimes committed in Kosovo as contended by the Prosecutor. It's an irresponsible contention. He did not raise any issue of possible crimes committed in Kosovo. He was just harping along the Perisic line about the unconstitutional use of the army in Kosovo. We all know there was no unconstitutional use. Mr. O'Sullivan clearly pointed out to you in his remarks that in that meeting when shown additional material, Djukanovic then indicated that he was satisfied with that. Another thing we heard about 1998 in Kosovo was that the VJ was using disproportionate force. One of the places you'll see it in the Prosecution's brief is in paragraph 709 where they refer to Naumann who said that Milosevic was presented with somewhere between five and ten incidents in which disproportionate force had been used. There's been no really thorough examination in this case of what that phrase means, "disproportionate force," and what it is. What we have is the opinion of some of the observers that were -- that were in Kosovo at the time that -- that they thought that disproportionate force was being used. And I've given a lot of thought to what that is. It's a strange concept in many ways. It makes sense if what you're saying is that you shouldn't use heavy weaponry against persons wielding spears and throwing rocks. I would agree that that force in that nature would be disproportionate. But I don't understand it to mean that the force you use must be roughly equal to the force that you're going against so that the same number of fighters are killed on each side. Clearly it can't mean that, but that seems to be what's being suggested by the Prosecution here, that the Serbs should have let the KLA kill more of their people instead of trying to deal with them the way they did. They argue that Serb use of tanks and artillery when terrorists didn't have any was disproportionate force, and I suggest to you that is not the law and was never meant to be the law, and again, pick a war, any war, and you'll find that that's not the case in any war. And how much more disproportionate could force possibly get if you apply that kind of a test to it than the dropping of cluster bombs on a country that had no effective air force and a rather ineffective air defence capability? Cluster bombs and uranium munitions, things of that nature. I mean, the Serbs weren't dropping cluster bombs on any NATO countries. I suggest to you you're not required to risk the lives of your soldiers in any way that gives advantage to a terrorist uprising. Terrorists were shooting at Serbs from houses, they were shooting at Serbs from even mosques on occasion, we've learned. And you have an absolute right to shoot back with a tank or an artillery weapon. You don't have to send your soldiers marching out across the field and have them mowed down by people in those buildings. I was going to talk to you about the I think absolutely ridiculous allegation in paragraph 104 that Ojdanic should have disciplined Pavkovic. Mr. Sepenuk covered that pretty well. What should he have disciplined him for? For what? Is there any evidence that Pavkovic was committing any crimes that he should have been disciplined for? Was there any evidence that he was doing anything he should have been disciplined for other than being an absolutely exemplary soldier and carrying out the orders that were given to him? You know, you have an obligation if you're an officer in the military to carry out the orders you receive unless those orders order you to violate the law. Look at every order in this case and you'll not find one that orders General Pavkovic to violate the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's some indication that, and I'll get into this in more detail, that maybe he was not properly reporting. I've already talked about the false allegation of illegal use of the VJ in 1998, so I don't know what it is that the Prosecution thinks Ojdanic should have disciplined him about. Ojdanic sent Vasiljevic and Farkas down to Kosovo, you know, to look at what was going on down there, and they came back and said, "Well, we found out that all the crimes that are committed down there are being detected and prosecuted. Ninety-five per cent of them are being prosecuted and there aren't any problems, none at all." It's paragraph 837, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk about another big issue of the Prosecution and that is the breaching the October agreements, and I suggest to you this is probably one of the more silly arguments that they make, because you know if you don't have evidence to prove your indictment, then you sort of figure out other -- other things you can accuse people of that kind of might make them look bad. You know, it's not against the law for the October agreements to have been breached. That is not an offence that is within the jurisdiction of Your Honours. They're not charged in this indictment with breaching the October agreements. I tell you it's a smokescreen. In paragraph 776 they contend Ojdanic facilitated the deliberate breaching of the October agreements. In paragraph 781 they contend that breaching of the agreements jeopardised a peaceful solution to the Kosovo problem. How? We all know what happened. When the October agreements came into force KLA took advantage of the Serb adherence to the agreements, expanded its forces, brought in new arms and equipment, retook much of the territory that had been taken during the spring offensive. Breaching those agreements didn't jeopardise a peaceful solution. The agreements themselves jeopardised a peaceful solution because they put the KLA back in a position of power, back in a position where they were carrying out the same kind of attacks against the Serbs and fellow Albanians that they'd been carrying on before. Even the Prosecution agrees that the KLA took major advantage of the situation. Mr. Hannis said on Wednesday the KLA came back just as strong or stronger than ever. He told you that in the context of suggesting to you that the 1998 anti-terrorist strategy was a failure and a new strategy needed to be found, but actually the 1998 strategy did work, and the October agreements came along, restricted the Serbs, gave the KLA a wide-open gate to walk through, and with Western help and encouragement they walked right through it. You may remember an intercepted conversation between two KLA members that's in evidence in this case. It's in our brief at paragraph 120, one of them saying to the other, now the verifiers have arrived. Things will be good. They don't dare attack us, but you attack them. Guard your houses at night. Go out in the field from time to time, carry out an attack and then return to the base. We learn a lot from that. Guard your houses at night means they were in their houses at night this these villages where they were being protected by the villagers. They'd go out and carry out these attacks and then return to those villages and then they wouldn't be wearing their uniforms. And it is exactly what we've been hearing the way they operated. And the OTP contends that Pavkovic was making up that the KLA was attacking Serb forces and just pretending that the KLA was attacking Serb forces, when they say exactly that's what they were going to do. We know the observers were not make any serious efforts to curb the KLA. And as Judge Nosworthy pointed out, when the Serbs entered into this agreement they must have expected that there would be some kind of parity between the opposing forces. They must have expected that the KLA would be restricted in some way as they were being restricted, that it really would achieve what the Western powers said they were trying to achieve there, that it would bring about a cease-fire and stop the war, and instead, what happened was the KLA was allowed to run wild and achieve the strengthening and rearming that was soon clear to everyone. Remember John Crosland's statement about that. Sometimes when I was sitting and listening to the arguments of the Prosecution I -- it sounded as if they were talking about the Serbs having invaded some independent third country, that they had illegally invaded an independent third country. I think we have to keep in mind that this was happening in their country. This was happening in Serbia, a place where their army had an absolute right to be, a place that was their place, and you know, just -- you all are from a different country in this world, and what would happen if an insurgent uprising like this started in your country? What if a bunch of terrorists started trying to take over part of your country? You'd deal with it, I suggest, in pretty much the same way the Serbs tried to deal with it here, to bring it to an end, to save their country. What the Serbs actually did in 1998 when they brought in some additional people, additional forces down toward the end there, may have saved a lot of lives. We have no idea what kind of a bloodbath may have occurred had the KLA simply been allowed to run unchecked throughout Kosovo because of those October agreements. And then one has to ask what's the relevance of violation of these agreements in this case? There could be relevance, I suggest, if the OTP could show that any additional forces brought in to Kosovo in violation of the agreements engaged in the commission of war crimes. There's absolutely no showing of that. There's no showing that any soldier or any unit brought into Kosovo in violation of the October agreements committed any war crimes. So it's just irrelevant smoke that's designed to obscure the issues in the case. They contend that Pavkovic on his own brought the 72nd Special Brigade into Kosovo without authority, and that shows you that Pavkovic on his own was violating the October agreements, but they only refer you to P1947, the document where Pavkovic suggests resubordination of that brigade to the Pristina Corps. They neglected to point you to P1948 which is the 19 February order of General Ojdanic where he orders the resubordination of that unit to the 3rd Army "for the purpose of carrying out anti-terrorist and anti-sabotage tasks." So again General Pavkovic is simply carrying out orders that he receives. And clearly, you know, it wasn't designed that they be on the edge of Kosovo. It was designed that they be in Kosovo "for the purpose of carrying out anti-terrorist and anti-sabotage tasks." You couldn't carry out anti-terrorist tasks outside Kosovo. It's another specious argument against General Pavkovic and they knew or should have known that it was a false argument. Paragraph 25, on a different subject now, of the brief of the Prosecution says: "All the accused shared Milosevic's sentiments about Kosovo and were loyal to him." And then this: "Some such as Nebojsa Pavkovic had close personal ties as well." And they cite you to Vasiljevic, P2600, paragraph 21. That statement of Vasiljevic says nothing about close personal ties between Pavkovic and Milosevic. What he speaks of is an indirect family connection which may have influenced the relationship. That's what he says, indirect family connection which may have influenced the relationship, not close family ties [sic]. Paragraph 137 the Prosecution talks about the removal of officers -- 72, line 15 I said close personal ties, not close family ties. Paragraph 137: "The SDC minutes provide," important words here, "concrete evidence that JCE members Milosevic and Milutinovic removed individuals who were unwilling to further the goals of the JCE from key positions and replace them with other accused who had shown their commitment to implementing these goals. Totally unsupported allegation of the OTP. Mr. O'Sullivan has discussed it at length and I'll touch on it very briefly. The OTP used the phrase concrete evidence. What is concrete evidence? That's evidence that's rock hard. It's unassailable. It can't be questioned or countered. They say this exhibit provides concrete evidence that Milosevic and Milutinovic removed individuals who were unwilling to further the goals of the JCE. I ask you, is this really a responsible argument? Is there anything in this document where they talk about removing persons unwilling to further their goals and replace them with those who will? Where's the evidence that Pavkovic was willing to implement the goals of the JCE? Zero. Nowhere does Pavkovic say oh, yeah, okay, I'll deport people and I'll kill people. If that's what you want, I'll do that. That's what you have to hear for this to make any sense. It makes no sense. He hadn't ever deported any Albanians before, hadn't ever killed or raped any before, to our knowledge. Where do they get the idea he was willing to carry out those goals? I think it's a desperate statement by a Prosecution that really has no concrete evidence at all. It's not even remotely logical. Paragraph 916, talking about Pavkovic again. He had the authority to immediately remove commanders and soldiers from their positions. During the war Pavkovic made daily visits to the field where he reviewed and inspected the units to assess the implementation of orders. Pavkovic also had the ability to remove volunteers who participated in criminal activity. Well, I guess the question you have to ask is when was it in the record we learned that Pavkovic became aware of specific named volunteers committing criminal activity that he failed to remove? When was it Pavkovic became aware of commanders ordering the commission of war crimes that he failed to remove? Where is the evidence that he became aware of specific soldiers committing war crimes that he failed to remove? Nowhere. Nowhere. And that has to be there or this makes no sense and has no impact. Why don't they say, if Perisic was telling the truth he had the authority to remove Pavkovic and didn't? Why don't they argue that? I want to go now to this whole issue of arming and disarming. Paragraph 872. Pavkovic engaged the Pristina Corps to monitor the behaviour of the Albanian population and disarm Albanian civilians along the border belt. Why -- tell me, why in a situation that existed in Kosovo at this time was it a bad idea to disarm Albanians who were in an uprising against Serbia? Why was that a bad idea? If you had that -- as I said earlier, if you had that kind of an uprising going on in your country, wouldn't you try to disarm the people that were involved in that uprising? How many lives were saved by the disarming of these people? How many lives were saved by removing weapons from the hands of possible KLA terrorists? You heard that little quote, the intercept, go out and conduct an action and go back to your village. That's exactly what they were doing, and the VJ was going into those villages along the border belt and taking those weapons out. So they weren't going out and conducting actions and then fleeing back to their villages like they said. Disarming them is what could bring peace and what could save lives. It's not a crime. It's sensible. How many lives would have been saved in Northern Ireland if the IRA had been disarmed earlier than it was? How many? Hundreds maybe? We don't know. We do know that terrorists didn't always wear uniforms. We know they were supported by and lived in the villages, and their effectiveness in killing Serbs and fellow Albanians who sympathised with Serbs depended to a great extent on the number of weapons they could get their hands on. Disarmament lessened this violence and the killings they could inflict, and lives absolutely must have been saved thereby. There is no evidence it was done so that they could be indiscriminately killed, which is the suggestion that's made by the Prosecution, I guess. There's no evidence of that. Paragraph 873. As early as June 1998, Pavkovic issued an order to organise local non-Albanian civilians into local defence units and to arm them with sniper rifles, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles and light machine-guns. Well, again a very misleading statement to you. The allegation is that Pavkovic did this, that it was Pavkovic's responsibility and that what he was arming was non-Albanian civilians. You already know from what you've heard at least in these arguments and probably in the trial that this was done due to an order that Pavkovic received from Samardzic and you heard that Samardzic detailed in a meeting how he had done this and how he had issued this order. What's misleading is the nature of the order itself. If you look at P1415 which is the order signed by Pavkovic, first of all you will see that he refers -- that he says it's being issued pursuant to the 3rd Army's previous order, 168-104, and then who is it he's arming? Paragraph 1, organise and carry out technical preparations for distribution of weapons and ammunition to military conscripts assigned to war units of the Pristina Corps, the Pristina military district and the 202nd logistics base. This is not non-Albanian civilians. It's conscripts. Are they suggesting you're not supposed to arm your soldiers? Is that the Prosecution's position, that it's illegal to do that? That's what that order was. Paragraph 126 talking about the armed non-Siptar population. The Prosecution makes this unsupported statement: "The absence of written orders setting out the task of the non-Albanian population suggest that field commanders issued verbal instructions to arm locals and directly organise these groups on the ground." Absolutely no support in the evidence for that, none. The transcript reference about it speaks only of the ability to issue tasks to secure certain facilities or features and roads, nothing more. Gergar, who was the one who testified about this, said there weren't even any non-armed Siptars in his whole area of responsibility, so he never even encountered the possibility of having them guard roads or certain facilities or features, but that's all they were ever intended to do in the first place. And again this is another one of these red herrings, another one of these puffs of smoke that's being blown your way. Where in the record is there evidence that crimes were committed by these people? None. And arming them is not a crime. It only becomes a crime if you arm them with intent to go and commit crimes and order them to do so and they go do it, and that's not here. If you just take the allegations that are made by the Prosecutor and turn them over and say so what was supposed to happen then, they get silly at times. You've heard about Pavkovic failed to report. Well, failed to report what? In the first place, they admit that it had no effect. Paragraph 740: "Despite failures in reporting by the 3rd Army command, Ojdanic received the relevant information from other sources." So it made no deference according to the Prosecution. And if it made no difference, then it makes no difference to you. It's totally irrelevant. I want to talk about, Judge Chowhan, your question to Mr. Sepenuk about this reporting issue a little bit. You talked about the Louise Arbour letter, for instance. I think it's really important to understand that that letter was sent on the 26th of March, the second day of the war. There is no way Louise Arbour could have had any concrete evidence about what was going on in Kosovo on the 26th of March. No way. The Prosecution in fact refers to it as a notice from Arbour basically saying, please understand we're paying attention, and if war crimes are committed down there, we're going to probably do something about it, and that's all that was. The other thing that's -- that's important with regard to this issue of reporting, Judge and Judges, the -- the duty to report with regard to crimes is a duty to report to the military prosecutors. That's who those are supposed to be reported to. That's what the law says and that's what all the witnesses told you. The crimes are to be reported to the prosecutors. The brigade commander is to report to the prosecutor. The brigade intelligence officer is to report to the prosecutor. The brigade security officers are to report to the prosecutor. And Vasiljevic and Farkas basically told you that, that what they learned was that the security officers at the brigade level were dealing with these crimes. They were being properly prosecuted, and they thought as long as they were taking care of it without any problem, they didn't have any obligation to report. Well, if they didn't report, then it didn't go up the security organ chain of command, which was a chain of reporting that existed, and you'll see it in our brief. There was a security organ chain separate from the army chain and outside the army chain, so they should have been reporting up that chain and they weren't. But that was their job. Their job was dealing with crimes and reporting those crimes to the military courts and reporting about those. What the combat reports were designed to report and what they were reporting at the order of General Pavkovic was the work of the military prosecutor's offices and the military courts and you'll see, and I've brought it up before with you, you'll see 3rd Army combat report after combat report after combat report which contains a paragraph on the work of the military prosecutor's office and the military courts, and that's what was required to be reported in the combat reports and that's what was reported. So there wasn't any failure there either. And there's absolutely no evidence in this case that at any time there was an abandonment of the Prosecution of war crimes. At no time did the military prosecutor say, oh, we're not going to prosecute any more. We're through prosecuting. We're done with this. What happened was this war ended. The Serbs had to leave Kosovo. A lot of the cases, because people were then leaving the military, had to be turned over to civilian courts. There was substantial chaos through that period, but you'll see if you look at the history since the war that there have been many, many prosecutions in civilian courts of crimes that were committed by soldiers in Kosovo during this war. So the Serbs never stopped prosecuting and never withheld prosecutions. They continued doing it. The allegation that Pavkovic didn't report these kind of things when he knew about them is defeated to some extent by the Prosecution's own brief. You know, when they're arguing against one of the defendants they sometimes give you favourable evidence with regard to another one. In paragraph 711 they're talking about Sainovic, and they say: "Pavkovic said that he'd informed Sainovic that he'd seen a group of Skorpions and Boca in Prolom Banja wearing NATO type uniforms and the insignia of the SAJ. Pavkovic said he'd ordered military organs to establish responsibility in respect to the bodies disinterred at Izbica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he had informed Sainovic of this. So there's Pavkovic when he knows something reporting it all the way up to Sainovic. Paragraph 555: "The necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish which a superior must take are those measures that are within his material possibility to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. In essence it is a commander's degree of effective control, his material ability which will guide the Trial Chamber in determining whether he reasonably took the measures required either to prevent the crime or to punish the perpetrator. Generally speaking, necessary measures are the measures appropriate for the superior to discharge his obligation showing that he genuinely tried, genuinely tried to prevent or punish and reasonable measures are those reasonably falling within the material powers of the superior." Now, you know, that is almost a description of General Pavkovic and who he is and what he did. He squarely fits in this category of person that they're describing. There are, I think, 27 orders from Pavkovic that were admitted in evidence in this case where he is ordering adherence to the laws of war, ordering adherence to the rules of war and suggesting that failure to adhere will result in swift and sure punishment. Twenty-seven times. Now, should he have done it 28 times? Is that the Prosecution's position? Or 30? What if he'd only done it 15? Would that maybe have made him guilty? Who knows. But I don't -- I don't think if you look at any other military commander in his position in the time-frame that this operated in that you would find 27 such orders issued by that commander. I don't think that's -- I think that's extraordinary. It's an extraordinary effort to prevent and punish. Your Honours, I think -- I think I could go ahead and break now if you want. I'll stay on this prevention and punishment thing for a little bit longer and maybe it's more than 10 minutes, so it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll adjourn now, Mr. Ackerman, and we will resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope everyone enjoyed their lunch. I did. I'm a little sleepy, yes, Mr. Milutinovic, I am. My colleagues told me I need to clarify one of the things I'd talked to you about just a little bit. I talked to you about the 27 orders that Pavkovic issued regarding adherence to the laws of war, and I know I mentioned earlier, I think I did, that one of the reasons for that number was new recruits were coming in all the time and he wanted to make sure that they were advised. Another part of that is that he was getting also orders coming down from General Perisic or General Ojdanic or General Samardzic to that effect that he was simply passing on in accordance with his responsibilities. So that effort was not just being made by Pavkovic, it was an effort that was going all up the line in the VJ, and so I think that clarifies that a bit, I hope. Now, paragraph 833, the Prosecution tells you with some alarm that Gojevic testified that only 12 per cent of the crimes prosecuted by the military courts related to war crimes, crimes against life and limb, the types of crimes charged in the indictment, and I say to you I think that is a high number, because most of what was going on that was being dealt with by the courts were the desertions and the failures to report and things of that nature. So if 12 per cent of the things they were prosecuting were crimes that were war crimes, could be seen as war crimes, crimes such as murder and those kinds of things, I think that's a high number and shows that the job was being done extremely well, especially when you consider that this all happened in a very compressed little period of time, and look how long it's taken us to get this case to trial. How many years has it been since the events happened in Kosovo before we got this case to trial, before the Prosecutor was able to get this case to trial. So the fact that they didn't try everybody within the 78 days of the war is meaningless. And they couldn't have done it. It's not possible. Paragraph 836: "Following his visit to Kosovo in June 1999, Farkas personally informed Ojdanic of this bottleneck in reporting. While Farkas testified that the measures were taken to punish perpetrators and the issue was simply the lack of reporting, then they say this is not credible in light of the disproportionally small number of prosecutions for serious crimes against civilians given the scale and type of the crimes alleged in the indictment." The same argument. Looks to me like they were doing a really good job if they were doing 12 per cent. We talk about -- the Prosecution talks about, you know, these people being replaced because they would do the bidding of Milosevic. Two people who were brought into the situation by Milosevic are two of the people the Prosecution relies on fairly heavily, and that's Vasiljevic and Farkas. They were both brought in by Milosevic. Were they brought in because they were willing to do his bidding, as they say, what regard to some of these other people, willing to carry out the JCE? If so, why aren't they sitting back here behind us also? These are people that were brought in by Milosevic that were sent down to look into the matter by Ojdanic and came back and reported exactly what they saw. There's no argument they had special relationships with Milosevic or that they were his cronies or they were covering for anybody. And when you are a military commander at the levels of Pavkovic and Ojdanic, you send people like that down to investigate things for you because you trust them to do it. You choose people you trust to do it, and there's no indication in this case that Vasiljevic and Farkas were not trustworthy in that regard. And when they come back and report to you, you're entitled to believe those reports. You're entitled to accept those reports. You certainly would accept them over what some journalist somewhere writes because he's been sitting in Brussels listening to Jamie Shea. That's about the worst evidence you're going to find is what Jamie Shea says in those stupid briefings in NATO. Paragraph 900, they're talking about Pavkovic's awareness of the commission of crimes. They say Pavkovic was aware of allegations of a mass grave in the area of Izbica in early April 1999. Pavkovic says he heard about it but was informed by his subordinates that no VJ personnel were involved, so he took no other action than reporting it to the SC staff. So he did everything he was supposed to do. What else was he supposed to do? He heard about it. He investigated it. People told him that nobody that he had effective control over was involved. He reported that he had investigated it and what his findings were. And again he's entitled to rely on those people he sends out to do those investigations for him. Paragraph 902: Orders issued by Pavkovic show that he was aware of the criminality of his troops. For example, on 17 April, he issue the following warning: "According to some reports, there have been a number of individual cases where the provisions or the instructions on conduct in combat or those of the international law of war were not fully adhered to in combat operations. Some commands and units have failed to devote the necessary attention to the suppression of incidents related to looting and crime." Exactly what he's supposed to do. When he hears about a situation like that, he sends out an order and he says, "I'm not going to put up with this. This has to end." That's what he's supposed to do. That's what the law requires him to do. That's what he did. 903: "In early May, Farkas and other members of the SC staff reviewed reporting within the 3rd Army. Farkas discovered that Pavkovic was receiving information about the criminal behaviour of his subordinates but was not passing that information up the chain. In order to clarify this situation, he met with Pavkovic." Again the OTP has got it wrong. If you look at the testimony, Farkas did not say that Pavkovic was receiving these reports and not passing them on. He said the reports were being made up to the level of brigades but not passed on from there. So the brigade level security people or brigade level commanders were not reporting those things on up into the Pristina Corps and then finally on up to the 3rd Army, up through the Pristina Corps. So Pavkovic couldn't even have known. Here's what Pavkovic says, here is his exact words: "Yes, there were differences and the difference was that some crimes were committed and some of the measures that had been prescribed had not been complied with. Reports in those units up to the level of the brigade were regularly reported to the superior commands, but this information never reached us, so I learned that criminal offences were being committed, crimes, including crimes in this area." And one of course always must wonder what would have been different if they were being prosecuted, if they were being punished, if the trials were going on at the highest rate they could possibly happen, then what relevance is the reporting? Paragraph 920: "As the military justice system was functioning well, according to the Prosecutor, the manifestly inadequate prosecution of perpetrators of crimes against ethnic Albanian civilians was clearly a consequence of the military's failure to report these types of crimes to the military courts." First of all this doesn't implicate Pavkovic. There is no evidence in this case that he was aware of a crime committed by a specific individual or group of individuals that he failed to report to prosecutorial authorities. The OTP has provided no list of persons who committed crimes against Albanian citizens that have not been prosecuted and prosecutions continue today even as we stand here. For this paragraph to have any relevance in this case and significance against Pavkovic, it was incumbent on the Prosecution to identify persons over whom Pavkovic had effective control who committed crimes who were not prosecuted and to show that Pavkovic had knowledge of these persons and their crimes and did nothing or suppressed that information. No such showing has been made with regard to any crime, not one. I want to talk about the crime base just very briefly because it's pretty heavily covered in our brief and in other briefs that you have before you, but in paragraph 312 the Prosecution talks to you about the rapes that were committed and just makes this statement: "The rapes were not isolated acts committed by individuals but were intended to terrorise the population and push people to flee their homes." There's absolutely no evidence that would support such a statement. Of course there were rapes. You're dealing with -- you know, just look at any war. You're dealing with young soldiers, not pillars of society especially, and these kinds of things just happen no matter what you do to try to keep them from happening, and frequently what they are is isolated indents that have nothing to do with the war itself but just out-of-control individual people. And to make that stick to anybody in this case, they have to go beyond just proving that rapes occurred. I abhor rapes. They shouldn't happen, but that doesn't mean that they become war crimes just because they do. 313: MUP and VJ seized the identification documents from the refugees in order to make it impossible for them to return to Kosovo. First of all, the seizure of documents was not a uniform thing, as you know. Obviously not a part of any plan or it would have been uniform, and as you pointed out the first day, Judge Bonomy, and I swear to you I had this in my notes before you pointed it out, Serbs could not have possibly believed that they were going to defeat NATO and thus keep Albanians from returning. That is a silly proposition beyond belief.
