utterances.text: We'll reach conclusions in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I suggested it was a conclusion. I didn't mean to do that. Perhaps some individual half drunk people standing at the border thought it would be a really cool idea to take away identity documents, you know, kind of a if you don't like Serbia then you don't have any right to have Serbian identity documents, but there wasn't any organised effort to pull that off or it would have been done a little better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a comment on this. When -- when Mr. Hannis comes to respond, it might assist us if he's able to identify who, if any, among the witnesses actually lost their documents. I appreciate there's plenty of evidence about this activity, but I'm not sure that any who actually gave evidence lost documents. There may have been some. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, I told you a little earlier that -- that one way to look at an allegation made by the Prosecution is just turn it over and look at the other side of it. Ponder what would have happened in this case if the Serbs had decided, "We better not let anybody leave Kosovo. We better close the borders and keep them all here or they'll suggest that we are guilty of deportation." So they closed the borders and keep all the Albanians in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem. Keep all the Albanians in the country while NATO bombs are falling down on their heads and several of them wind up getting killed. Then we'd be defending a human shields case, wouldn't we? The Prosecution would say, well, they kept them in the country to use them as human shields. They wouldn't let them go to safety. Frankly, I see nothing wrong with the Albanians being allowed to leave that country, even being encouraged by some to leave that country because there was bombing going on. It was dangerous. It was not a safe place to be. And so you get away until it's over and then you come back. I think there's 2 million people that have left Iraq. Nobody made them leave. Thousands and thousands left Ossetia when the Georgians decided to go in there. They're now starting to return even today. You just don't have wars where bombs are being dropped where you don't have refugees. It just doesn't happen. People are people, people get scared. They try to get away, they want to run away, they want to get away from what's happening. There is no crime regarding the passage of the Albanians across the border. There was no deportation. It was clearly the safest thing, considering what was happening. And everyone knew when the war was over they would be coming back, those who wanted to. Some want to stay in other countries and that's where they are. Paragraph 318 is where the Prosecution starts going through the crime base, the evidence regarding the crime base. Frequently what you see in there is the phrase that this was done -- this was committed by the forces of FRY and Serbia. General Pavkovic didn't have effective control over the forces of FRY and Serbia. This is a failure of proof. When the Prosecution says forces of FRY and Serbia, what they are saying to you is it was committed by unidentified persons. We don't know who they were, so we'll call them forces of FRY and Serbia. And that may even be wrong. Look at the one incident we talked about today, that Norman talked about today that they had in their brief about these people being killed and it was finally discovered it was done by civilians and civilians were prosecuted for it. And I suppose if we didn't know who they were, then the Prosecution would call them forces of FRY and Serbia. In other words, unidentified persons. 362: The beginning of the joint VJ/MUP operations coincide with the crimes committed in the Prizren area and with attacks on the villages of the municipality, and then this sentence: There simply were no other significant armed forces in that area at the time the crimes in the indictment were committed." No support for that statement at all. How would they know that? They weren't there. They presented no evidence about it. 627: "The mass killings and other crimes committed in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 were of such magnitude and covered such a wide area that they could not be kept secret and were widely known." Well, I don't know of any evidence that they were widely known. I think most of them were discovered after the war was over when they were able to get in and talk to witnesses. I don't think there was any widely known about it. There's certainly no evidence of that. In the initial arguments of the Prosecutor, Ms. Kravetz was telling you about the trains from Pristina, about people being transferred by trains from -- from Pristina, I'm sorry. She says, this is her language: "These civilians were transported by train to the Macedonian border, and as we've heard from several witnesses, including Mr. Bucaliu who worked at the Urosevac train station during the last week of March and going into the first week of April, the frequency of trains travel from Pristina to Orahovac and on to the Macedonian border was increased and so were the number of cars on the trains in order to be able to deport larger numbers of people out of the province." Again not true. Bucaliu's testimony on 8 September on cross-examination by my colleague Mr. Aleksic, Judge Bonomy asked him what he was -- why he was going into this since there was a log, and Mr. Aleksic says he is he trying to prove that in that period 25 March to 3 April nothing was happening. The trains were not operating for five days and after that, there was only one train in two days. There was not a major increase in terms of trains, and Judge Bonomy says, well, you can just make those submissions in argument. I don't think anyone's arguing with you about that. And Aleksic says thank you and Judge Bonomy says, well, carry on with your question so he does. And he says, Mr. Bucaliu, in this document that you explained to us in detail there's no information about the number of passengers and number of train cars; is that right? "A. Unfortunately, yes, it's true. There's no number for the carriages and for the passengers." Ms. Kravetz told you on page 14 of the first day the Defence have advanced several different possible explanations as to why the population left. We heard that the arguments in the sense that the population left because there were NATO bombing, the KLA was forcing them to flee, and we heard arguments that they were fleeing because there was fighting going on. We say that these reasons do not explain why the population left. Well, we sat here at 98 bis and heard Mr. Hannis tell us, 12594 in the transcript, "We're not saying that some of these people didn't leave because of the bombing. We're not saying that some of these people didn't leave their villages because they were told to do so by the KLA." So it wasn't just Defence that was making those arguments. It was Mr. Hannis himself who was telling you that people were leaving because of NATO bombing and leaving because of being told to do so by the KLA. The problem, of course, is we don't have any numbers as to how many left because of NATO bombing and how many left because they were told to do so by the KLA, and we don't know if that is a number that exceeds 10 even for sure, because to even believe it exceeds 10, you have to accept the testimony of people who might have a reason for telling you that story. At page 3510 of the first day's transcript, I think it was the first day, yeah it was, Judge Bonomy asked Mr. Stamp what he was saying about the responsibility for the Meja killings. Mr. Stamp responded that it was the evidence of Pnishi and Peraj and Dedaj that people were killed by both the VJ and the MUP, and this is simply not the evidence. Paragraph 586 of our final brief details that evidence. Pnishi did not describe VJ as committing any killings. Peraj says the VJ was not involved in killings, not even near where the bodies were found. The only witness who even begins to implicate VJ was Witness Dedaj, who told at least three different stories at different times about what she'd observed and whose evidence I'd suggest to you is not capable of being accepted, certainly not as proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Mostly from Prosecutor Stamp but perhaps from others you kept hearing the phrase massive crimes, the massive crimes that were committed in Kosovo. Now, Your Honours, I'm familiar with what happened in Rwanda where a million people were killed, at least. I'd call that a massive crime. I'm familiar with what happened at Srebrenica where maybe 8.000 people were killed. I'd call that a massive crime. But I think in the context of this case, massive crime is a major exaggeration, major exaggeration. It doesn't apply to Kosovo. Of course there were crimes. Every war has crimes, but this was not a case of massive crimes. I want to talk about the Joint Command for just a moment. Paragraph 201, the Prosecution says "Although the composition of the Joint Command changed in 1999 as Minic and Matkovic were no longer in Kosovo, Lukic, Pavkovic and Lazarevic remained members of the joint command." There's absolutely no evidence to support that. They don't even -- they don't even put a citation there to anything. They just say it. Even if there was an active frequently meeting Joint Command in 1999, and I suggest there was not, but even if there was, you must understand that Pavkovic was no longer the commander of the Pristina Corps. His participation in that Joint Command in 1998 was as commander of the Pristina Corps. I think Samardzic maybe visited those meetings twice throughout that entire period. I haven't counted it up. But once he went up to the 3rd Army it would have not made sense for him to be part of those meetings because they were tactical, they weren't strategic, and he was now a strategic officer. But that -- that statement that they remain members of the Joint Command is just simply unsupported. The only thing that could even remotely support it is when Vasiljevic says he went down there in June and went to a meeting and Pavkovic was there and Lazarevic was there, but that doesn't necessarily support that they were members. Pavkovic could have been doing what Samardzic did on a couple of occasions and that is attend those meetings, and he happened to be in the area. Paragraph 228 the Prosecution argues this to you about the Joint Command: "Once authority to proceed was issued by the Joint Command, they would each task their subordinates to provide the required units and to liaise with their respective counterparts in the VJ and MUP at the VJ brigade or PJP detachment level where the ground level details of the plan would be finalised." I don't think that's the paragraph I want to refer to. Somewhere here I think it says that Pavkovic would carry out the orders of the Joint Command and that's the part that I'm trying to refer to. And I think it's important that you pay particular attention to Exhibit 4D91, which I think is one of the most significant documents in this case, as Mr. Hannis would say, one of my favourite documents. This is the -- the order from Samardzic to Pavkovic of 30 July 1998, ordering him -- detailing his duties with regard to this Joint Command. He tells him that prior going -- to going to the meetings, he must tell the chief of staff about any requests, possible requests, and explain proposals for the engagement of forces with reinforcements. And then after he gets consent to agree to some of those proposals or disagree, whatever, he then goes to the meeting, but he goes to the meeting armed with approval from the chief of staff who Samardzic has delegated to take over his duties there in the forward command post. Then after the meeting he's required to report back to the army chief of staff on the proposals that have been accepted or any other subsequent requests which diverge from the proposal and shall ask him for permission relating to those requests. And then he has to inform the Joint Command of any decisions made by the Chief of Staff regarding those requests. So he was never allowed to do anything that was suggested or proposed by the Joint Command until he got approval from General Samardzic or his deputy, the chief of staff. That's what that order says, and that's a really important order. I think Mr. Fila covered this, but Mr. Stamp elevated Djakovic to membership in the Joint Command and there is simply no evidence that he was a member. He was there taking notes. If you -- if you look at the beginnings of those meetings where it lists the members present, Djakovic is never listed as a member present. He wasn't a member. He didn't say he was a member. On day two of arguments is when Mr. Hannis talked a lot about the Joint Command as if there's something sinister about this Joint Command, if it's something criminal and shady and sinister, and there isn't. In the United States we call it the Joint Chiefs Of Staff. In your countries your military organisations all have a comparable organisation, because forces must coordinate their activities. The United States Army, when being supported by the United States Air Force, needs to talk to the air force about what they're going to do and when they're going to do it and how they're going to do it. They have to have joint meetings, coordination meetings. Every military organisation in the world has a coordinating body similar to what was created here to deal with this war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I imagine the membership of any such body would be recognised, Mr. Ackerman, but here we have a dispute about whether people are members or not and certainly some accused contending that there is no such identifiable body. It's not a straightforward comparison in the cases of some of the accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only speak for one accused, Your Honour, and I speak from what I see and what I think the evidence shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's a mistake to -- to try to oversimplify it to us, those with no experience of -- of direct experience of the work in Serbia and the FRY at that time when those who do have that direct experience seem not to have the same views about its nature. I think that -- I use the word "nature" in a more general sense than a more specific term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to hold my tongue, but I will. There's something I'd love to say to you that I don't think I should. But I will say this: You have to understand that -- that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in the process of creating itself when this all started happening. It had been Yugoslavia, and then it was no longer Yugoslavia. It became an entity only encompassing Serbia and Montenegro. So they had to rewrite all their laws. They had to rewrite their constitution. They had to rewrite everything. And you don't always get it right when you're just starting brand new. You do make mistakes when you're starting brand new. That accounts for why the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal have been amended 37 times or something because they didn't get it right the first time. And you can find anomalies in those first rules. You'd say how can this be. Well, it could be because it was a brand new organisation just starting out and they just didn't quite get it right the first time. So you have to understand that this was a work in progress, this creation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that will help you maybe understand why the rules of the SDC and the constitution regarding the SDC seem to be in some conflict, because it was still being created, and that was why there was nothing within the security forces like we might see in our countries like the Joint Chiefs Of Staff in the United States because they didn't have an opportunity to consider how they were going to deal with coordination between all the different parts of the security forces there. So it was an ad hoc thing, I think, that was put together here at the last minute when they realised that they had to keep from shooting even other. And how it was organised and who was in it and what it means in this case remains of course to Your Honours to figure out and understand, but I don't think it's a sinister body in any way. There's no evidence. Read those -- read those notes all you want. There's no evidence that they were carrying out some of a JCE. There's no evidence that they were planning the commission of any crimes. And my colleague Aleksic suggests that you also keep firmly in mind that you're dealing with -- with two sovereignties here to some extent. The VJ was a federal institution under federal control, the MUP was a state institution under state control, under Serbia rather than FRY. As to the continuation of the Joint Command into 1999, the Prosecution has referred to -- to that meeting where everybody is talking about how and whether it's going to continue and what form it should continue into 1999 and so forth. Just remember that General Pavkovic, P1468, page 160 said it was his view that the Joint Command should cease to exist. I'm going now to paragraph 891. By late March 1999, Pavkovic was aware of the mass movement of civilians. He also was aware that identity documents were being confiscated from ethnic Albanians who were leaving the territory. The first thing I will say about that is mass movement of civilians does not automatically equate with crime. NATO was bombing in March. Common sense tells us that people flee from bombing and common sense would have told Pavkovic that in 1999 also. Second is his awareness of the confiscation of identity documents. The OTP cites his statement but fails to mention that he went on to say that after he learned of it, he investigated it and learned that the army was not involved in it at all. The army was not the border police. It's clear that he was determined to make an end to it if it was being done by persons over whom he had effective control, but it was not. Paragraph 893. It's under the heading Pavkovic knew of the crimes committed by forces of the FRY and Serbia operating in Kosovo in 1999, and there's a report that 32 criminal reports were filed against perpetrators of crimes on the preceding day. That's a report from the courts, and those are the reports that Pavkovic ordered that he receive, and what you're seeing there is that crimes are being processed, being prosecuted. Criminal reports are being filed. That means they're being referred to the courts, and they're saying that's evidence against Pavkovic, but it's actually evidence for Pavkovic if it's being done. There's an argument there that while the military's reporting crimes of attempted murder and murder and abuse and things like that, the report that goes up about that from the 3rd Army doesn't say that, and you know, those are obviously two different reports, two different situations. Just because they both happened to be 32 criminal reports, they're talking about totally different offences, and it wouldn't make any sense for anybody to do that to try to cover anything up, anyhow, because the courts were reporting straight up to the General Staff on their own outside the normal chain of command anyhow. There is an allegation, I can't tell you what paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, just very briefly, could you clarify one reference for us, P1468, you referred to General Pavkovic's view that the Joint Command should cease to exist, and you gave a page reference from P1468. Could you give us that again? The transcript says 160, but there aren't 160 pages and I thought you said 60. But it's not on page 60 either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My note says 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I don't know if there's 160 pages. Mr. Hannis talked about it so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think there were 163 or 164 pages in the English and it's either 160 or 161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're referring to the English then. All right. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's an allegation in the Prosecution's brief and I seem to have misplaced it, but it deals with the allegation that -- that Pavkovic knew about crimes being committed by volunteers in -- throughout the brigades or something like that. If I don't have the exact language here, I don't really want to rely on it, but it refers to a document, and what that document shows, it's P1938, on page 2, is on 1 April 1999, after only a few days, 25 volunteers were returned from the Pristina Corps. Seven were detained for rebellion, killing, robbery, rape, insubordination and desertion. Two killings took place, one volunteer and one woman volunteer were killed. Now, this doesn't show some wide knowledge of crimes by volunteers. It's one group of volunteers in which a few people were causing trouble, seven, actually, and they were all returned back and taken out of service. So what was done there is exactly what should have been done there, and that's not evidence of any crime on the part of the General Pavkovic. Paragraph 202, and this comes from P1281, page 2, the police had their own headquarters headed by their own officers. This is Pavkovic. And the cooperation with the army was coordinated through political actors in Joint Command formed for the purpose. Therefore, the information to what police force units were doing can best be provided by the police commanders and the members of the Joint Command in charge of them. And the Prosecution cites that as evidence against Pavkovic but what it really shows is that Pavkovic had no control over members of the MUP. They were not persons that he exercised effective control over in any way. Paragraph 870: Pavkovic used his subordinate units to commit crimes. There's no evidence of that. There's no evidence he used his subordinate units to commit crimes. Just because crimes may have been committed doesn't prove this kind of a statement. They need to prove knowledge and intent. We know that American and British soldiers committed crimes in Iraq. That doesn't lead us to conclude that British and American generals used them to commit crimes. You'd have to show that they intended for them to commit crimes, that they sent them there to commit crimes, not just that they did it. If -- if commission of crimes all by itself was enough evidence to make leaders and commanders guilty, then all of our military commanders would be in gaol and we would have a problem with our armies with no commanders, you know. I'm going to try to finish up, Your Honour, because I think I'm out of time. One matter that I think is interesting and I think significant also, paragraph 288. The Prosecution points out the evidence of Baraybar, who concludes at that gunshot injuries were inflicted on persons that were not participating in combat activity. Mr. Stamp talked to you about that in his arguments the other day. When I saw that it just struck me how could you possibly know that. How could you know that somebody with a gunshot wound was not engaged in combat activity, so I looked into it. The problem with that testimony is that Baraybar based his findings on statistics from other combat situations and on two kind of interesting variables. First he said that if these persons had been in combat there should be been more shrapnel injuries and less gunshot injuries. Well, yeah, that would be true in a maybe typical war situation where weapons other than rifles are being used, but if it's a war situation where only rifles are being used, then it has no meaning at all. Rifles don't produce shrapnel. So as a result, if it's only rifles, there would be few or no shrapnel injuries in a pure rifle fight and that wouldn't prove that these were persons who were killed not involved in combat activities. The second thing he said, and his words are interesting, he said you usually don't see the types of gunshot wounds found here in combat situations where the fighters are wearing body armour. It is the case that KLA often fought out of uniform, you know that, and that they weren't wearing body armour. They didn't have all that -- well, all that fancy body armour and all that kind of fancy equipment and stuff. So again taking the statistics from other wars in other conditions with other uniforms and other equipment and trying to apply it to some bodies that he's looking at that have bullet holes in them and say he can draw meaning from that is just ridiculous and it shouldn't be accepted by you. So while the conclusion is maybe statistically correct regarding what he looked at from statistics from other wars, it has no meaning here. It will certainly not support the statement "The inescapable inference is that forces of the FRY and Serbia murdered these persons during the execution of JCE," which is what the Prosecution tells you. It's far from an inescapable inference. And as I said, forces of FRY and Serbia means unknown persons. There's no evidence that these deaths were the cause of any kind of a JCE. In paragraph 271 the Prosecution says paramilitaries were engaged in combat operations with VJ units. I think there's no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you kindly slow down for the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 850, and this is an example of why I tell you to pay attention to the footnotes: "During the indictment period Pavkovic reviewed the work, order and discipline of all units of the Pristina Corps and those subordinated to it. Footnote 2129 referring to P1078." P1078, Your Honours, is a report for the year 1998. It says absolutely nothing about 1999. So it didn't have anything to do with during the indictment period. Paragraph 888: "Another frequent topic at Joint Command meetings was arson," and they mention one statement by Sainovic in August, and I thought gee, that doesn't sound like it being a frequent topic. So I did a search as best that I could, and I found there were actually four such references in the 164 pages of those notes, and I don't know whether that makes it a frequent topic or not, but what's important is that every time it was mentioned, it was mentioned in the context of this is outrageous, this can't happen, this must stop, we can't permit this. Not you're not burning enough houses, go burn some more. So it's preventive language that you're seeing, not permissive language. That entire paragraph, by the way, of the OTP brief doesn't speak of plans to commit crimes but efforts to prevent crimes. Paragraph 271 of their brief shows Pavkovic ordering people to take care in anti-terrorist operations so as not to damage residential buildings, and that order was issued on the same day that Sainovic mentions there was a problem in that regard. I think the Pavkovic order probably went out before Sainovic made that remark since those meetings were in the evening. Paragraph 905. Paragraph 905 the Prosecution is talking about the indictment against Milosevic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ojdanic being made public, contained detailed allegations about deportations, forcible transfers, rapes, murders and so forth and that this put Pavkovic on notice of the widespread nature of alleged war crimes. And then they say the next day Pavkovic got a report from Lazarevic about the failure of MUP to be resubordinated to the VJ, and then the following day Pavkovic wrote his report, P1459, which is the subject of some dispute, but the Prosecutor's position on that is that was written in response to Pavkovic learning about the indictment against Milosevic et al., and I suggest to you that that's simply not true. The indictment against Milosevic et al. was not made public until 27 May. If you see our brief at paragraph 240 you'll see there was a court order entered in that case ordering that it not be made public until 27 May and we've referred to it in our brief. I've come, Your Honours, now to a page that it says conclusions on the top of it. I want to -- before I go directly into that, the other thing you have to keep in mind, I think, as you review this evidence is that this wasn't a situation like we have here where we can sit around for hours and contemplate things and think about things and make decisions about things and then take another day and think about it again. This -- this stuff all happened in the chaos of war, and the chaos of war is not a place where it's easy to deal with your day-to-day operations, and so of course people made a mistake here and there and of course things got dropped through the cracks because communications weren't always what they should have been. So just in the back of your minds remember the chaos that war brings. I want to for the record adopt some portions of briefs of my colleagues. Milutinovic 117 through 182 -- no, actually 117 through 244 of Milutinovic, 12 through 151 of Ojdanic. Now, Your Honours, until Tuesday and Wednesday of this week I'd spent two years believing that what we were trying here was a war crimes case, and then Tuesday and Wednesday I learned that it was something else altogether. It's a case about the misuse of the VJ in Kosovo in 1998, a case about the violation of October agreements. It's a case about failure of reporting. And these are the things we heard as we listened to the Prosecution's final arguments. What we didn't hear was who were the persons who committed the crimes contained in the crime base. Who was their superior? Did that person know they'd committed those crimes? Did that person report it or cover it up? Did General Lazarevic know about it if they were VJ members? Did General Lazarevic tell General Pavkovic? Did General Pavkovic fail to see that it was reported to military prosecutors? That's what makes a war crimes case, and that's not what we heard in this courtroom, ever, not ever. What we heard was massive crimes were committed. The people in this room on the accused bench occupied high positions. General Pavkovic took prevention measures but not enough. General Pavkovic took punishment measures but not enough. That's not a war crimes case. It's not a case at all. Mr. Hannis wants you to apply Occam's razor, look at the evidence and the simplest explanation is the right one, the one you should adopt, mostly likely alternative he wants you to adopt, and I know as I said he wishes that's what the law was. Mr. Hannis said you should follow the maxim of if it looks like a duck and walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it must be a duck. Well, I was -- I'll tell Hannis a story. I was in front of a crusty old county court judge in Texas one day with a motion to suppress some evidence in a case, and this is a guy who had been on the bench for years and smoked cigars on the bench and didn't wear a robe, and the prosecutor on the other side was a young female lawyer, and I argued my motion and she argued their position, and he looked at her and he said, Little Lady, that dog won't hunt, and that was his ruling, and that's what this case is about, Your Honours. This dog won't hunt. That's not evidence here upon which you can convict General Pavkovic. I urge you not to do so. I urge you to do your duty, do what's right and acquit him of all the charges against him. Before I sit down I want to say a thing or two on a kind of personal level. I've had the great privilege of appearing before the Judges of this Tribunal now for 11.5 years, almost as long as Mr. Fila has. I share his feelings about that. It's -- it's a part of my life and a significant part of my life. A fourth of my life as a lawyer has been spent in this court, but I look back on it with a great deal of pride and a great deal of appreciation, and I'd be remiss if I sat down without thanking this Tribunal and its staff, its Judges, its Prosecutors, its translators, all of the people who have taken part in making this just a truly memorable experience for me. You have let me join a very small club, and that includes the four of you up there on this bench today. I was aided in this case by a very able co-counsel, Mr. Aleksandar Aleksic from Belgrade, and I know he also appreciates his opportunity to be here, and I appreciate all the assistance that he provided to me in this very difficult case. I have to leave The Hague tomorrow, Your Honours, so I won't be here with you next week, and so this is kind of my last hurrah. You might remember that I once told you that where I really wanted to be was up on a mountain top breathing clean air and having a rest. That's where I'm going. It may not be a mountain top. It might be a golf course, but it will certainly be a place where I'll be able to relax. I just want to invite everybody in this room to come there with me, and all you have to do is come to Texas and ask around and maybe I'll see you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for these submissions, Mr. Ackerman, and since we won't have the opportunity to say anything to you at the end of the case, we thank you for the way in which you have conducted the defence of your client and the dignified way throughout in which you have contributed to what for the Judges, too, has been an extraordinary experience. We shall now proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We should proceed to hear the submissions for Mr. Lazarevic but perhaps you would clarify first of all for us, Mr. Bakrac, whether there would be any prospect of him being here on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still do not know that. My colleague Mr. Cepic and I had planned upon the close of this session to go to visit him. What I do know is that he is still in the detention centre hospital, but I'll be able to fill you in on the details subsequently once I pay a visit to him. But I don't think that there are any problems in us continuing the proceedings, in continuing our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue with your submissions, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all of you, you and everyone else in the courtroom, and I know that especially after Mr. Ackerman's closing arguments at the end it will seem an ordinary phrase, something that more experienced colleagues have said before me, but nonetheless I would like to address the Trial Chamber. It is up to me now, so I would like to express the great honour and privilege and pleasure it's been to defend General Lazarevic before this Tribunal, before this Trial Chamber and in these proceedings. It was also a pleasure and privilege to present before you, although I'm not sure that you -- to be able to hold forth before you, although I'm not sure that you always had the pleasure of listening to what I had to say. But I do sincerely hope that this portion of the courtroom will have the pleasure of hearing your final word and be satisfied by that. Before I go on to my closing arguments, I'd like to inform you that our Defence team has accepted the Prosecution tactics, although we know and believe that it won't be successful at the very end, but anyway, with your permission I'd like to inform you that I'm going to address you with -- by saying -- or responding to Mr. Hannis's closing arguments, and my learned friend Mr. Cepic will be speaking to you on the subject of the brief of the sixth Defence team and crime base details, and so with your permission, at the very end I would like to take the floor again to speak about the state of consciousness of my client, his state of mind, and all the evidence that we have produced and the decision and proposal for judgement. My learned colleagues before me for the most part spoke about a thesis put forward by the Prosecution with respect to the joint criminal enterprise, and so I should just like briefly to add some of my own observations on that subject with respect to the evidence that was presented before this Trial Chamber. The Prosecution claims that the goal of the -- of the joint criminal enterprise was to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo by resorting to criminal means in order to ensure further Serbian control in the territory. Now, apart from a sentence uttered to that effect and a sentence which is found in the indictment and which is echoed in the final brief and the closing arguments, we have not heard from the Prosecution in what way this change in the ethnic balance would ensure further Serbian control over the province. We have not seen the nexus between this undertaking and endeavour to throw out a portion of the Albanian population, to expel the Albanian population, and the further, better easier, or more comprehensive exercise of control over the province. I think the Prosecution was duty-bound to provide us with information of that kind and to explain to us the background, the substance of such a vast criminal enterprise that they allege. Now, I'd like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to certain facts, facts which are stipulated by the Prosecution in their written submissions. The Prosecution claims that at the time relevant for this indictment in Kosovo there were about 1.700.000 or 1.800.000 Albanians and that is to be found in paragraph 44 on the Prosecution's final brief. According to the Prosecutor, and this is to be found in paragraph 81 of the indictment, in Kosovo there were between 5 to 10 per cent Serbs. That is to say the ratio between ethnic Albanians and ethnic Serbs in 1999 at the time relevant for the indictment was 90 to 10. In his closing arguments of the 20th of August this year, Prosecutor Hannis was very decisive in stating that the Prosecution claims that the intention of the accused was not to expel the entire population but a significant portion, and they also claim that 700.000 to 800.000 is that significant portion of the population and that that was precisely the intention of the accused. On the assumption that the claims made by my learned friend Hannis are correct, in this new population constellation in which we would have 1.100.000 Albanians and between 150.000 and 200.000 Serbs, we come to a new ratio of forces, between 80 per cent Albanians and 20 per cent Serbs on the assumption that the Serbs did not leave the province. Now, I would like to raise the following question for the Trial Chamber: In what would way this new ratio of forces substantively alter the ratio of forces which would secure further Serbian control over the province? We have not received an explanation, let alone the fact that there has been no evidence to show that at all. The Prosecution has not provided a shred of evidence to bear that thesis out for us really to be able to see whether or not it was in fact a goal and whether an undertaking existed in the first place. We say that these allegations made by the Prosecutor as to the object of a criminal enterprise or joint criminal enterprise already on first blush are out of the question. There is no sense to them. On the other hand, there are many witnesses and other written evidence presented before this Court which quite obviously create and paint a completely different picture about the reasons that the Kosovo Albanians moved out of the territory and not only them but others too. The Defence dealt with this in greater detail in its final brief in paragraphs 483 up to paragraph 505, and I'd just like to mention some of that evidence now and to point the Trial Chamber to them. For example, a Prosecution witness, Sandra Mitchell, on page 588 of the transcript testified and said that up until the 20th of March, 1999, she was the acting person in the OSCE mission and that the plan for supervising the refugees was made only on the 22nd of March, because the problem of refugees was one that they did not have up until then. This plan quite obviously if you look at the time period coincides with the intimations of NATO bombing and the departure of the OSCE mission from Kosovo. This witness also adds and says that the Serb civilians also left the province at that same time. Adnan Merovci, another Prosecution witness, testified in this court and said that on the 21st of March he saw refugees moving towards the border, towards Macedonia and that is to be found in Exhibit P2588, paragraph 43. Another Prosecution witness, otherwise the chief of staff of the AKM, Bislim Zyrapi, in his testimony on transcript page 5991 to 5992 and 5997 to 5998 states that the civilian Albanian population was moving together with the KLA and confirms that he issued an order personally ordering the movement and shifting of the Albanian population from the village of Bellanice on the 1st of April, 1999, that is Prosecution Exhibit number P2457. Another Prosecution witness, General Drewienkiewicz, also testified and said that P680 evidence was correct to the effect that in the region of Djeneral Jankovic the KLA ordered the civilian population to move out, which they did, and this can be found on 7932 page of the transcript. There were many Defence witnesses who testified to these circumstances as well but through -- but because our time is limited I'm just going to mention Milutin Filipovic, for example, and a number of them. He testified that on the territory of Pristina and the surrounding parts there was a distribution of handouts, pamphlets in Albanian in which the KLA called upon the civilian Albanian population to leave Kosovo and Metohija and go in the direction of Albania and Macedonia. The transcript page is 11984. All this evidence and all these exhibits lead us to conclude that part of the population left the province because of intimations of a coming NATO bombing or because of pressure and instructions from the KLA whose aim it was to show that there was a humanitarian catastrophe and the responsibility of the Serbs for that catastrophe, and the results of that kind of conduct are quite evident and obvious today. If we bear in mind the standards adopted at this Tribunal to the effect that this kind of thesis put out by the Prosecution can be considered to have been proved if the Prosecution's conclusion is the sole reasonable conclusion that one can draw, we consider that it is quite obvious that the Prosecutor has failed to prove his thesis about the existence of a plan and the existence of a plan to prove it beyond reasonable doubt. In addition to that, in addition to the fact that these exhibits and the evidence shown about what the true reason for the moving out of the Albanian population was, if we look at it, at first glance what makes more sense is this, more sense than the Prosecution thesis and the joint criminal enterprise thesis is -- and that the goal was to change the ethnic balance allegedly to enable Serb control of the province. Here and now I don't wish to deny the fact that there were individuals who to certain -- did say to certain Albanian civilians, go to Albania or go to Clinton or something similar. My learned friend Mr. Ackerman talked to you about this, because there was a war on and much worse things happened, killings and rapes for example. And it is quite true and to be expected that some individual might have said things like that to Albanians, but they are isolated verbal incidents which in -- can in no way be proof and evidence of the existence of a plan as presented by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor then goes on to suggest the following: That from the orders of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, Grom 3 of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, Grom 3, that from them other orders emanated which under the mask of the struggle to break up the Serb -- Siptar terrorists represent a coordinated action on the part of the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP directed against the civilian population and that the areas in which the fighting took place and the battles took place in fact coincide with the areas in which the alleged crimes happened, the crimes cited in the indictment. And on the basis of that he draws the conclusion that this is clear proof of the existence of a plan. The Defence claims that this thesis put forward by the Prosecution has remained at the level of speculation and surmise and that there are no indicia, no indications or any proof which would show beyond reasonable doubt or which would confirm this position taken by the Prosecution beyond reasonable doubt. Before I continue -- before I continue my presentation on these orders and directives, I'd like to show the Trial Chamber of the contradictions to be found in the closing arguments presented by the Prosecution with the intent of showing these decisions as being a screen behind which crimes were committed. My colleague Mr. Hannis, on page 8 of the transcript of the 19th of August, speaking about these orders and the orders which were titled Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, stated that ever since World War II, for example, this kind of plan is never written down -- or, rather, never documented, nor is it ever declared orally by any side. However, a little bit before that, on page 3 of that same transcript, my learned friend Hannis asserts that Mr. Milosevic, in October 1998, to Generals Naumann and Clark, openly stated that the final solution for the Kosovo problem will be found in the spring by doing the same thing that happened in Drenica in 1946, that is to say will rally them all together and execute them. Now, we're not quite clear, but that seems to be the Prosecution thesis, does it. Now, why, if Mr. Milosevic quite openly told high-ranking NATO officials what the plan was for the spring, why then would these orders be screened for conducting something like that? There is quite obviously a contradiction here in what the Prosecution has presented. The Defence furthermore claims that the stipulated orders of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, Grom 3 of the 3rd Army, Grom 3 and the Pristina Corps, for the defence of the country and for fighting the KLA were completely legitimate and legal and that these orders and the orders that emanated from them in no way were used to mask plans that were targeting the Albanian population. There is a lot of evidence to show clearly and unambiguously that this -- it was justified and necessary to elaborate directives and orders of this kind. And the Defence spoke about this in greater detail in paragraphs 605 to 628 of its final brief. Every serious army, every serious organisation, even without the kind of threats that we're going to describe in our further presentation has a defence plan, necessarily has a defence plan, necessarily adopts a defence plan. This building has a plan for evacuation should a fire break out, for instance. So why, as Mr. Hannis would have it, would that be something that was necessarily adopted to mask and hide a plan that was directed against the civilian population? Let me remind you that it was precisely a Prosecution witness, Dusan Loncar, who said that the KLA used the presence of the KVM to reorganise, consolidate, arm and prepare for the struggle against the Serb forces. And the witness added that the KLA very often used civilians as a human shield, principally women and children on page 7617 of the transcript and goes on to testify of that while he was in contact with General Drewienkiewicz, what was often mentioned was the forthcoming spring offensive by the KLA and this is to be found on page 7618 of the transcript. Another Prosecution witness Shaun Byrnes testified before this Trial Chamber that all the international observers in Kosovo were generally aware of the fact that the Albanians armed themselves before, during, and after the October agreement. Page 12217 to 12218 of the transcript. Another Prosecution witness, Ciaglinski, confirms that the KLA, during negotiations held in Paris intensified its attacks. Page 6902 of the transcript. Another Prosecution exhibit, P638, for instance, which represents a report of the OSCE mission under the marking DZ 5 of the 8th of January, 1999, shows that the terrorist KLA attacks and the violation of the truth undermined efforts for a political solution to be found to the conflict. Another OSCE mission DZ 16 this time, Exhibit P649, which represents information from a meeting of the liaison officers with representatives of the KLA, resulted in the following conclusion: That regardless of what was to happen in the next round of the peace negotiations, there was the clear readiness on the part of the KLA to continue their fighting. There are also numerous reports coming from the security organ of the Pristina Corps and of the 3rd Army pointing to the same facts. We ask the Trial Chamber to inspect these documents that's 3D1050, 3D1052, and 3D1053. 5D1241, another exhibit, is a BBC video clip showing military manoeuvres by the KLA on Mount Drenica in the village of Klecka on the 29th of January, 1999. And here you can also see fighters in civilian clothes and women carrying weapons. General Lazarevic testified about this on transcript page 17771. In addition to all this, the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia had at its disposal intelligence indicating that in Macedonia in early 1999 about 10 to 12.000 NATO soldiers were deployed with about a hundred tanks and 36 helicopters, and it was estimated that NATO was planning an air and ground operation. NATO air-strikes were announced in February 1999, and Mr. O'Sullivan spoke about this in his closing arguments. From the territory of the Republic of Macedonia, there was an increased influx of KLA and weapons with a view to creating a corridor. 3D1048 and 5D253 are exhibits illustrating this and pointing to this. In this kind of military and political situation it was completely natural, logical, and legitimate for the army to adopt plans, directives, and orders for the defence of the territory and of the state sovereignty both against the NATO forces whose possible aggression was being prepared and which actually took place as we have seen, and from the KLA which was acting from within with great force. When one analyses the Pristina Corps command order, P2808 shown to you by my learned friend Mr. Hannis, and it's dated the 16th of February, 1999, for the destruction of the Siptar terrorists in the Malo Kosovo area, which is also known as Lab or Podujevo, Drenica and Malisevo, and 455-1 is the log register number, one can see that in addition to the purely military tasks assigned to the corps units the corps commander General Lazarevic prohibited the entry of members of the court into built-up areas and he warned the members of the corps that they must not violate international -- the international laws of war. If you look at P2808, you will see that all this can be found there. I ask the Trial Chamber to look at another piece of evidence which supports all of this and which perhaps shows in the most impressive way the fact that all these orders were justified, but the exhibit is under seal so I ask that we move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bakrac. We can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document we refer to shows clearly and unambiguously that the orders and commands referred to were adopted in -- that it was justified to adopt them. Another witness from the Pristina Corps testified that in addition to the large concentration of KLA on the territory of Malo Kosovo Drenica and Malisevo, this area was suitable for a landing by the NATO multinational force and their linking up with KLA. That's 21817. That's the transcript page. This general order, 2808, is one that individual orders were based on bearing the heading Joint Command for KiM and General Lazarevic testified that these were orders of the Pristina Corps command and that these were actions in support of the MUP. My learned friend Mr. Hannis also mentioned these orders, saying that they stemmed from this order, P2808, and that they corresponded to the territory from the indictment referring to the crime base. We will show that these orders, of which we have 16 as exhibits on the record, only 4 of them correspond to the crime base from the indictment. That's P2015, P1968 and P1969, and P1975. If you look at the territory from the crime base as described in the indictment and compare this with the remaining 15 orders -- rather, excuse me, the remaining 12 orders, you will see that these orders refer to actions in areas where no crimes were committed. If these were orders which were intended to mask a plan to commit crimes against ethnic Albanians, the question arises why only four of these orders relate to the crime base? Why not all of them? And the answer is clear. It's clear because the OTP has no evidence to support its case and is engaged in speculation. A simple analysis of the contents of all these orders shows that there was a legal and legitimate sequence both as regards the content of the orders and the chain of command. In addition to this, the content of these orders leads quite clearly and unambiguously to the conclusion that they are not a screen or a cover to commit crimes against Albanian civilians under the pretext of fighting the KLA as the OTP contends. We wish to remind Your Honours that General Vasiljevic, a Prosecution witness, was shown an order issued by the Pristina Corps commander, P2014, and that this witness, Vasiljevic, evaluated this order as being a typical document composed in a precise and professional manner and that it's a high quality document. That's transcript pages 8732 and 8734. My colleague Mr. Ackerman has already mentioned, and I have noted down that here I would agree with my colleague Mr. Hannis who asked you to apply the principle, and I'll tell you the following: If something is called an order and if its context shows that it is a high quality order, then probably it is an order and not something quite different. Your Honours, I now wish to move on to another topic, and I see we have only two minutes left, so I don't know if this might be a convenient moment, and -- I do apologise, Your Honours. My colleague Mr. Cepic has received an e-mail. Mr. Lazarevic is still in the prison hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. We will adjourn at this stage until Monday. We're due to sit on Monday morning. We will have to interrupt the sitting at around 11.45 or thereabouts because there is a Plenary meeting of Judges that the Judges here are required to attend. If by then we know that there is other time available on Monday, we may take advantage of that, and similarly on Tuesday. We may try to -- well, we are trying to secure other time, but it may prove impossible because of the commitments of other cases, but please don't take on any commitments on the assumption that we will not be sitting a little longer on Monday and possibly for part of Monday morning -- Tuesday morning, but we will alert you as soon as we can of any change to the sitting arrangements. For the moment, we shall resume on Monday at 9.00 and sit until 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of August, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24
